With Benjamin Netanyahu ramping up warnings of fresh threats from Iran, opposition voices warning of potential disruption to the ballot, and Israeli rights activists warning of a further spike in violence by settlers in the occupied West Bank, political instability at home could leave Israelis facing both a fresh test of their democracy, and fresh security threats.
Why Israel's election is one of the most important in its history
Israeli voters are preparing to head to the polls in an election some have described as the most consequential in the country's history.

It's the first general election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023. Tuesday's vote could see Benjamin Netanyahu's almost two-decade-long period of right-wing rule replaced by a more left-leaning government.
Emerging as Netanyahu's main challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, who says the election is about Israel's identity as a liberal and tolerant democracy.
Netanyahu has made security central to his campaign, warning that electing his rivals would risk making Israel less safe.
Middle East correspondent Lucy Williamson reports.
The independent MP, who sits next to Haines in the lower house, said “there is a link between our words and actions”.
At a press conference shortly before question time, Steggall said:

I did not feel that Angus Taylor read the room when it comes to the lesson that Helen would like us all to learn. To make what’s happened to her, the utter tragedy of it, make sense to all of us, makes sense for Australia, then we have to be able to take responsibility for the impact our words and our debate has beyond the walls of Parliament. And the same goes to the words and the images and the editorials used in media, social media ... what ads we authorise at election time for a party.

These were all part of Phil [Haines]’s speech to us this morning, his words to us, asking us to raise the bar so that when Helen does come back to this place, there’s been a meaningful shift in how we can have a respectful debate.
We can disagree respectfully, but words matter and have an impact.
Big Build royal commission to hold public hearings through much of the Victorian election campaign
The royal commission into allegations of corruption on Victorian government construction sites is set to hold two weeks of public hearings in the middle of the state election campaign.
The inquiry updated its website on Monday afternoon confirming the first block of public hearings from November 9 to November 20.
This falls during the caretaker period, when the election campaign is expected to be in full swing, and includes a few days of early voting, which opens on 18 November.
Labor MPs are bracing for potentially damaging allegations.
Here’s what the royal commisison heard on the first public hearing last month:
Government accused of ignoring lessons from robodebt

An algorithm used by the federal government to assess the level of care older Australians are entitled to is unreasonable, unfair and lacks human oversight, according to a damning investigation by the commonwealth ombudsman.
The investigation also found transparency recommendations from the robodebt royal commission have been ignored.

The investigation followed reporting by Guardian Australia that older people were being left distressed and without adequate care after their home support needs were assessed by an “inhumane” algorithm as part of the government’s mandatory Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT).
Aged care assessors are barred from overriding the IAT’s funding package recommendation, even when the decision is wrong.

Documents released under freedom of information reveal departmental panic, severe clinical distress among frontline assessors, and secret IT workarounds after officials realised in the hours before the rollout of the algorithm that legislation legally barred human override, and that this was causing distress within days of implementation.
The shadow health minister, Anne Ruston,said the report shows: “The algorithm must be scrapped.”
Labor defended this system for months while the Coalition and the crossbench said it was broken. Today the independent umpire has agreed with us.
NSW police minister says gun buyback reflective of ‘very sensible approach’ by government

The NSW police minister, Yasmin Catley, and police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, held a press conference earlier today to detail the state’s gun buyback program. As we reported earlier, eligible licence holders are now able to book an appointment to surrender any excess or reclassified firearms from next Monday, 2 November.

Catley said bookings were essential as the buyback program began, saying people cannot walk into police stations without an appointment. Those who do turn in eligible weapons will receive compensation ranging from $450 to $1,000, depending on the firearm. Small businesses affected by changes to gun laws will also be eligible for grants up to $25,000.
A second phase for high-value firearms will begin next year.
“This has been a very sensible approach by the government,” she told reporters.
A very sensitive way of responding to the worst terrorist attack that we have seen on our streets in this country.
When asked about a draft proposal to allow some to apply for more than 10 firearms in limited circumstances, Catley said people would need “a very good reason”, such as competitive sport shooting.
“If you are at those elite levels, then it may be the case that you do need more than the 10 guns,” she said.

The alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines loomed large over the House of Representatives, creating a civil yet sombre question time. Some politicians offered compliments to their counterparts across the aisle, others contributed by keeping their derision for dixers to themselves.
The government faced questions on the sale of Victoria Barracks in Sydney.
The impact of social media on violence against women, workers and politicians came under the spotlight.
There were no ejections and just one warning.
It is yet to be seen whether this question time atmosphere will last more than one day.
Helen Haines granted leave of absence until at least end of sitting year
The independent MP for Indi, Helen Haines, has been given leave of absence until 26 November after she was injured in an alleged attack in her electorate.
The leader of the House of Representatives, Tony Burke, clarified he had simply chosen the last sitting date of the year:
Obviously, we will continue to move resolutions for as long as Helen needs us to.
No leave of absence motion stops the fact that, if at any moment, Helen feels she’s ready to come, then obviously she immediately will.
Continuing from the previous post, social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, says the tenor of public debate has changed significantly during her three-decade long political career.
It is more violent in its tone, and I think the industrial scale of the abuse that all of us receive – but particularly the women here receive – that has changed.
But I’d say this about social media … Social media companies profit by the division they drive in our society.
And that’s why all of us have a responsibility to resist that too. To resist that division, to resist the violence and discourse, that the big tech giants are forcing on us.
Tanya Plibersek is asked if public life is safe for women
Independent for Bradfield and the electorate’s first female MP, Nicolette Boele, directs a question to the longest-serving female member of the House of Representatives, Tanya Plibersek.
Violence against women, whether physical, spoken, or in writing, is used to silence them. And when it keeps women out of this place, it decides to represent us. That is not democracy.
What does the minister say to the young women of Australia now, wondering whether public life is safe for them?
I’m not surprised if there are young women all over Australia looking at the horrific [alleged] attack on Helen Haines, and wondering whether a life in public is worth it, whether it’s safe for them.
And what I would say to them is 100% it is worth it.
Every single day in this place, we make important decisions that change this country and change it for the better.
We can’t vacate the field to the people who would stop us from doing that.
Greens leader expects Steele-John to remain on leave until investigation complete

Greens leader David Shoebridge says he’s “glad” Jordon Steele-John made the decision to stay away from Senate estimates after a week of confusion following the release of a letter accusing him of inappropriate behaviour.

Over the weekend, Steele-John said he would not attend parliament next week after seven members wrote to Shoebridge urging an investigation into claims he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.

Shortly after the letter’s release to parts of the media, Shoebridge said Steele-John would go on leave while an independent investigation took place. Steele-John publicly rejected the idea that he was on leave.

In a press conference before question time this afternoon, Shoebridge said other members of the Greens will ask questions of the departments and agencies involved in the NDIS when they appear later this week. He added he would not go into a “blow-by-blow discussion about the exchanges”.
Asked whether Steele-John would remain on leave until the investigation is complete, Shoebridge responded:

Well, I’ve made it very clear to Senator Steele-John what I believe the community expectations are. If you ask me tomorrow, I’ll say the same. If you ask me the day after it, I’ll say the same. I’ve made it very clear what I believe the community expectations are.
Online radicalisation involves mixed ideologies, with violence the ‘only principle’, Burke says
Home affairs minister, Tony Burke, is asked a dixer on how the government is working with neighbours and partners to keep Australians safe.
He says all countries are now dealing with the radicalisation of young people:
Every country is reporting a new cohort, and growing fast, of young people, particularly male, where we used to worry about people becoming involved and radicalised in their teens.
The radicalisation [is] happening online and involving mixed ideologies.
Ideologies that would be completely incoherent with each other, but only having violence together as their only principle.
I want to assure the House of the cooperative work that Australia is doing with all of our agencies and all of our effort.
Bolsonaro says it is 'impossible to concede' poll result
Far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro said it was “impossible to concede the election result” and that his legal team would seek to have the election annulled.

Following in the footsteps of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who four years ago also refused to acknowledge his defeat by Lula – before attempting a coup and being convicted for it – the senator cited a supreme court justice’s decision to extend voting hours as the alleged reason.

Although Bolsonaro had also requested an extension of voting hours, the senator said Justice Cristiano Zanin’s decision to extend it from 5pm to 7pm “was not normal, it was unacceptable” and amounted to “changing the rules of the game while the game was being played”.

Bolsonaro said the decision had come from “Lula’s friends on the supreme court”, pointing out that Zanin had previously represented the leftwing president as his lawyer and had been appointed to the court by him.

The justice ordered the extension minutes after 5pm, the scheduled closing time for polling stations, after fellow justice Kassio Nunes Marques spent hours without ruling on Lula’s campaign request. During the campaign, Marques, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro and current head of the electoral court, had been criticised for bias in rulings favouring the far-right senator.
I’ve just been speaking to Lula’s overjoyed health minister, Alexandre Padilha.

“This is a huge victory for the Brazilian people who in the second round had the chance to think about what President Lula means for the environment, for the defence of our national health service and our education system and for the Brazilian constitution,” he told me, clutching my hand with emotion as he spoke.
And [to think about] the risks that the extreme-right candidate [Bolsonaro] entailed.
It’s a massive victory, not just for Brazil. It’s also an important signal to the rest of Latin America and to the world.
Tens of thousands of Lula supporters have poured onto Paulista Avenue at the heart of São Paulo to celebrate his historic election win.

The mood is of absolute ecstasy and relief after Lula managed to stage an unprecedented second-round comeback against his far-right rival Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro.
As fireworks blasted into the night sky, a group of revellers hoisted a sign reading “Dictatorship never again” onto the roof of one of the avenue’s metro stations.
“I feel amazing. Brazil is fucking incredible. Lula is our father,” said Leonardo Machado, a 44-year-old Lula supporter as he hit his city’s most famous street to toast the president’s triumph.
It’s nearly 1am in Brazil now and the party looks likely to go on until sunrise.

Lula’s dramatic win is bad news for former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence and was hoping to be freed and given a role in government had his son Flávio Bolsonaro prevailed in the poll.
Jair Bolsonaro was jailed for plotting a coup against Lula after the leftwinger won the 2022 election against him.
Lula’s win in this runoff election is also a blow for Donald Trump, the Bolsonaro clan’s most important international ally.

The US president had been hoping Bolsonaro would become the latest in a series of pro-Trump leaders to take power in Latin America, including Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia, Daniel Noboa in Ecuador, José Antonio Kast in Chile and Javier Milei in Argentina.
There’s more from Tom Phillips and Tiago Rogerohere.
More political leaders internationally have reacted to the news of Lula’s win against Flávio Bolsonaro.
The relationship between Canada and Brazil has flourished under our partnership.
Let’s seize this opportunity to make it even stronger, together – to create major new trade opportunities, protect the environment and build greater prosperity for both our peoples.
I congratulate President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva ... and salute the Brazilian people for this democratic day.
Our region has common enemies, shared challenges, and much to gain when we work together.

I just spoke with the President of Brazil, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Chile and Brazil have a lot of shared future ahead, and we will continue working on an agenda that strengthens relations between our countries in economic integration and the fight against organised crime in the region.
See here for our earlier post on the reactions of other leaders in the region and beyond – including Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum and Cuba’s Miguel Díaz-Canel – also care of Reuters.

There is a mixed mood on the streets of Brazil tonight, a few hours on from Lula’s historic victory was announced. In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.

But Rodrigo Valentim, a 51-year-old businessman and supporter of Bolsonaro, said that another Lula government would harm the economy. He pointed to financial markets’ positive reaction to the result of the first round, when Bolsonaro bested Lula.
“I don’t understand how people can vote for Lula,” he said. “The country is collapsing.”
Many have focused on the supreme court ruling extending voting by two hours, with Aurelio Junior, 45, a dentist in Brasília, calling it a “disgrace”.
We’ve never had anything like this in Brazil, and now they’ve come up with the idea of extending the election period by two hours.
However, Jacqueline Maria Lima de Franca, 34, a business owner in Rio de Janeiro who backed Lula, said it was “more than fair … everyone should have the right to vote, and that was being neglected”.
The Guardian’s Tom Phillips was in the São Paulo conference hall as Lula addressed a packed crowd of ecstatic supporters.
“I am [nearly] 81 … and I am going to do the best term a president has ever done,” Lula vowed.

We are going to change the way that this country is governed … This election was a defeat for denialism … I want to thank God and to thank you, Brazilian men and women of this country … it was democracy that made this happen.
Lula’s vice-president, Geraldo Alckmin, told the crowd:
You saved Brazilian democracy for the second time. Congratulations president Lula.
The president’s supporters chanted back: “Olé. Olé. Olá! Lula! Lula!”
US senator Bernie Sanders has congratulated Lula, saying he has “stood up for Brazilian workers and democracy”.
“Congratulations to Lula on his extraordinary reelection victory in the Brazilian presidential election,” the senator, who is a key figure on the US left, wrote soon after the results were clear.

The president of Brazil’s electoral court, Kassio Nunes Marques, has recognised Lula’s victory, saying “with more than 64 million votes, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has been re-elected and will be the 40th President of the Federative Republic of Brazil, for the term beginning on 5 January 2027”.
Marques added that he had called both candidates.

To President Lula, I express the electoral justice system’s recognition of his participation in yet another democratic process and of his victory at the ballot box. His political career spans different periods of Brazil’s democratic history. He has stood as a candidate in eight elections, winning four of them.
To candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, who contested a presidential election for the first time and received a significant number of votes, I offer my congratulations on his campaign.

In a five-minute speech in which he took no questions, and which appeared to have been deliberately timed to begin only after Lula’s televised victory speech had ended, Flávio Bolsonaro made no mention of the fact that his campaign had also asked the electoral court to extend voting hours.

While Lula’s request concerned cities in at least nine states where voters had not been provided with the free public transport guaranteed by law, Bolsonaro justified his request by citing heavy rain in some states.
As well as refusing to concede, the senator told his supporters:
I will not give up on my Brazil, and I hope you won’t give up either.
A birthkeeper who allegedly “groomed” pregnant women to fear hospital could be referred to prosecutors to face potential criminal charges, a Victorian coroner has heard.

Stacey Warnecke died in September 2025 at Frankston hospital in Melbourne after giving birth at home and suffering a postpartum haemorrhage with birthkeeper Emily Lal by her side, having paid her $6,000 to support her throughout pregnancy.
Birthkeepers have no clinical training and operate outside the medical system.
The inquest into Warnecke’s death began in June, but closing submissions to coroner Therese McCarthy were delayed after a forensic analysis of Warnecke’s phone.

Hearings resumed on Monday, when Rachel Ellyard, in her role as counsel assisting the coroner, said that the completed analysis had revealed numerous messages, including in a group chat on the platform WhatsApp coordinated by Lal for women who were choosing freebirth. A phone call between Warnecke, a 30-year-old nutritionist and wellness influencer, and Lal was played to the court.

Ellyard said the phone evidence directly contradicted evidence from Lal, given in June, that she was hired by Warnecke primarily to play the role of a supportive friend, and that the money paid to her was primarily for her time, but not for medical advice.

“Ms Lal saw her role as to groom her clients into being strong enough to resist the temptation to seek medical help during labor, to seek pain relief during labor, to go to hospital during labor,” Ellyard said.

“It’s clear that Ms Lal thought that in most cases, going to hospital would represent a failure of someone who hadn’t done the work, who hadn’t understood enough what the intensity of labor was going to be.”
During the call, Warnecke told Lal that she envisioned having a “wise woman” next to her during her first childbirth, to guide her when asking: “Am I dying, or am I alright?”
Warnecke told Lal she was afraid of the hospital.
Lal responded: “You should be scared of the hospital.”
“It’s a terrifying place. For me personally, I think the biggest, the key … to actually staying home and having your baby … is that your mindset and your condition needs to be so solid.”

Lal also told Warnecke that midwives who attend home births sometimes inadvertently sabotage them, because if the birth goes on too long, they tell the woman to go to hospital. This is sometimes just because the midwife is exhausted, Lal said.
She told Warnecke: “I manage my own energy as much as I can in that way, so that I don’t subconsciously sabotage a person.”

Lal previously told the court that she was not clinically trained, and that it was not her responsibility to make Warnecke’s birth safer, or to call an ambulance unless specifically asked. Lal said she never gave Warnecke medical advice, and only shared her own experiences of freebirthing her own children.

Ellyard said on Monday that given the evidence from the call and many messages and documents obtained from Warnecke’s phone, “the role that Stacey thought Ms Lal would play during the freebirth … was to help her by keeping her safe”.
“Stacey was placing considerable reliance on Ms Lal, in whom she had placed considerable trust.
“Ms Lal was an expert. She was providing advice. She was providing referrals. She was selling supplements. She was offering commentary.
“This is all quite inconsistent with the idea of just being a friend who pulls your hair back and wipes your forehead. It’s something much more structured, much more deliberate.”
Ellyard said Warnecke’s husband, Nathan, had also been “reassured or indoctrinated into a sense that his role was just to just sit back and support, and that whatever Stacey experienced was alright”.
Lal was invited to return to court to give further evidence after the phone analysis, but had declined to, the court heard.
Lal only gave evidence previously on the condition that the coroner grant her a certificate of protection so that her evidence could not be used against her in any future proceedings.

Ellyard put to the coroner on Monday that it would be open to her to find that Lal had committed perjury “in relation to the falsity of the evidence” and to refer her to the Office of Public Prosecutions.
The OPP prepares and conducts criminal matters on behalf of the director.

“Having regard to the materials that have now become available … it would be open to your honour to form the view that Ms Lal wasn’t truthful in the evidence that she gave to you, and that a referral could be made in relation to the offence of perjury,” Ellyard said.

She said there was also evidence Lal had been “holding herself out as someone capable of giving such expert advice and capable of meeting the needs of pregnant women in a range of circumstances” despite having no authority.

The court previously heard that Lal had asked Warnecke three times whether she wanted an ambulance called after she gave birth to the placenta, lost up to 1.5 litres of blood, then began struggling to breathe.
Lal previously told the court that it was not her role to call an ambulance against her client’s wishes, even if the woman was unconscious and dying.
Warnecke said yes to an ambulance the third time, but by the time paramedics arrived she was seriously unwell, having suffered a massive postpartum haemorrhage.
Warnecke died in hospital several hours later from related complications, with the hospital exhausting its blood supply trying to save her.
Ellyard said on Monday: “Stacey would have survived if she was in hospital.”

Midwives and doctors know that postpartum haemorrhage is the most common complication of childbirth and are so well trained to identify it and treat it that “women do not die in hospital” from it in well-resourced countries, Ellyard said.
Warnecke also “would have survived if she was giving birth at home with a registered midwife,” Ellyard said, drawing from evidence given by medical professionals earlier in the inquest.
“She suffered a known complication of childbirth, which was eminently treatable if identified and responded to immediately.”
The coroner will deliver her findings at a later date.
After a bizarre 2025 season, the Kansas City Chiefs are right back at the top of the NFL in 2026 and already well on their way toward yet another Chiefs-Bills AFC Championship game.

But last year's Super Bowl Champions, the Seattle Seahawks, have been far less convincing. After opening the season with two wins over the New England Patriots and Arizona Cardinals, Seattle entered the weekend just 1-3 since. The surprising loss to the Commanders was followed by a win over the hapless LA Chargers, then two frustrating losses to the San Francisco 49ers and Denver Broncos in overtime.

Last weekend's loss was ugly enough that speculation started immediately afterward that Sam Darnold might be in danger of losing his starting job to Drew Lock. From Super Bowl winner to backing up Drew Lock in six games? It sounds crazy, but that's what going 27/51 with no touchdowns and two interceptions, in a losing effort to a quarterback with 107 passing yards, does in the NFL.
Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald was adamant, however, that he'd stick with Darnold.

"Sam's played great football for us this year the majority of the time," he said in an October 16 radio interview. "There's other times he needs to take care of the football, but I think these are solutions we can find with Sam as our QB. I believe that."

"I think we have a lot of faith in Sam," he added in a news conference that same day. "Sam’s played great football for us. He’s done a lot of great things this year. We’ve obviously turned the ball over more than we want to. I feel like there’s things on our end that can help him play better football. And I think he’s definitely part of the solution, rather than the opposite."
He, and Seahawks fans, are probably glad Macdonald stuck with him. Despite some further, back-breaking struggles with ball security.

After a punt-filled first quarter, the second provided a lot more action. While Patrick Mahomes uncharacteristically struggled, with an interception killing a Chiefs' drive, Darnold was on fire for Seattle. On the Seahawks' first scoring drive, he threw for 71 yards, including a 33-yard completion to Jaxson Smith-Njigba. The very next drive, after Mahomes' interception, Darnold found Smith-Njigba again, connecting on a 28-yard touchdown pass thanks to some impressive strength from the 24-year-old wideout to stay in bounds.
In the waning seconds of the second quarter, though, Darnold's ball security issues crept up again.

After yet another big 28-yard completion to Smith-Njigba to put the ball at the Kansas City 2-yard-line with 30 seconds left in the half, the Seahawks tried a George Holani run that went backwards. Darnold, under pressure, tried to find Rasheed Shaheed in the endzone, only to get picked off by Noah Williams.
Williams added a lengthy runback, seemingly setting up the Chiefs for an unlikely, last-second score.
But Harrison Butker, not off to his best start thus far, missed the 58-yard field goal to end the half.

In the third, Darnold was back at it again, completing passes of 17, 12, and 19 yards to help Seattle add three points and make it 13-0. And the typically dominant Chiefs offense just didn't ever get on track. Mahomes was frequently hurried, and with Rashee Rice once again out, there was little separation from the Kansas City receiving corps. Kenneth Walker couldn't get much going on the ground either.

Mahomes was far from his best either, nearly losing a fumble in the third quarter, and mostly dinking and dunking his way down the field. Even when the Chiefs finally put together a solid drive in the fourth, Butker missed his second kick of the game, just a 45-yard try, that would have narrowed the score to 13-6.
Seattle took advantage, putting the game away with a 21-yard touchdown run from Emanuel Wilson on third-and-4.

While Lumen Field is a tough place to play, the level to which Seattle dominated Sunday night's game was still surprising. Prior to garbage time, they had a 388 to 210 yardage advantage with 22 first downs to Kansas City's 11. The Seahawks went 11/15 on third downs too, compared to just 3/11 for Kansas City. Kenneth Walker, coming off a game in which he had 19 carries for 128 yards and two touchdowns, went just 14 for 36 against Seattle. And the three points for KC entering the fourth quarter was tied for the fewest of any game in Mahomes' storied career.

It was the type of suffocating defensive performance that's become a hallmark of the Seahawks' run the past few seasons. And perhaps even more encouraging, a much better outing from Darnold, awful second quarter interception aside.
The Seahawks stay home to host the Chicago Bears on Monday night, while the Chiefs travel to Denver to take on the Broncos at Empower Field.
Oklahoma City Thunder star Jalen Williams was stretchered off the court against the Los Angeles Clippers after a gruesome left leg injury that appears it could end his season
Williams elevated near the hoop with Clippers defenders around him to attempt a shot when he landed in a very awkward position and seemed to fall with his left foot and ankle underneath him.
Williams’ reaction said it all, as his foot was not in the correct position.

As Williams put his head in his hands out of pure disbelief, his Thunder teammates couldn’t believe what they saw as well. Trainers quickly made a circle around him and assessed the situation following the brutal injury, which below is quite graphic to look at as a fair warning.

Williams was placed on a stretcher and wheeled off the court, where the Thunder faithful were chanting his name. He delivered a thumbs-up to the crowd to acknowledge their support, but everyone including Williams knows this injury isn’t going to be something he comes back from anytime soon.

The injury details still need to be disclosed by Oklahoma City, and yes, not all gruesome injuries lead to a season-ending one, but considering what the video showed, there’s a high likelihood that Williams’ 2026-27 NBA season is done before it really got going.
Williams entered his fifth NBA season, where he wanted to continue his role as one of the main stars on this loaded Thunder squad.
The former All-Star averaged 17.1 points, 4.6 rebounds and 5.5 assists across 33 games last season.

Unfortunately, Williams dealt with nagging injuries last season as the Thunder were trying to repeat as NBA champions. He dealt with a right wrist injury on his shooting hand, followed by right and left hamstring strains that caused him to be out for much of Oklahoma City’s postseason run to the Western Conference Finals.
While the Thunder won this battle with the Clippers to remain undefeated in the early season, they will need to find answers for the loss of Williams.
What also doesn’t help is guard Cason Wallace suffered a left shoulder injury in the first quarter of this contest before Williams went down. So, that’s two starters dealing with injury woes.
Alex Caruso, the versatile veteran who comes off the bench for the Thunder, and Jared McCain are likely the next men up for Oklahoma City.
Republican New York gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman blasted Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul as a "puppet" of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a campaign rally Sunday.

Speaking at the event in Yorktown Heights, New York, Blakeman, the current Nassau County executive, accused his opponent of embracing the democratic socialist mayor's agenda while failing to crack down on illegal immigration and crime.
"Kathy Hochul, she was out campaigning with Mamdani this week," Blakeman said, according to the New York Post. "And I say that’s great."

"Please take him everywhere you go, Kathy, because I want to remind people that this un-American, antisemite, anti-Christian mayor is running the Democratic Party and Kathy Hochul is nothing more than his puppet," he continued.
Hochul has been campaigning alongside Mamdani, including at a recent rally in Brooklyn.
The political alliance between the mayor and the governor, who is seeking reelection to a second full term, comes as democratic socialists have gained greater influence in New York politics.

Along with Mamdani's victory in last year's mayoral election, candidates aligned with Mamdani and New York's democratic socialist movement scored major victories in congressional primaries this year, including the defeats of two Democratic incumbents.
Blakeman has previously targeted Hochul and Mamdani over public safety, accusing both Democrats of failing to address crime in New York City.
During a campaign appearance on the city's subway system earlier this month, Blakeman described Hochul as the "most pro-criminal governor" and accused both leaders of failing to keep commuters safe.
Mamdani has also publicly criticized Blakeman, accusing the Republican gubernatorial candidate of engaging in "bigotry and racism" following a debate between Blakeman and Hochul earlier this month.

"I think the governor did a good job," Mamdani told reporters when asked about Hochul's response to Blakeman's criticism. "And I'll never fault someone for not being able to catch all of it because that is a fool's errand when it comes to Bruce Blakeman."
Hochul and Mamdani have emphasized affordability and child care while campaigning together, arguing their policies are aimed at lowering costs for working families.
Fox News Digital has reached out to Hochul's and Mamdani's offices for comment.
Fox News Digital's Eric Mack and Anders Hagstrom contributed to this story.
Brazil's left-wing President Lula elected for fourth term

BRASILIA, Brazil — In a stunning political comeback, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has been elected president of Brazil, according to official results from Sunday's runoff election, with more than 96% of the votes counted.
Lula secured more than 51% of the vote, defeating Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, who received more than 48%.

The result marks a historic moment in Brazil's democratic era. Since democracy was restored in 1989, no candidate who failed to win the first round of voting has gone on to win the presidency in the second round.

The victory also adds another chapter to Lula's long political career, securing him a fourth, nonconsecutive presidential term. Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, will be among the oldest sitting leaders in the Americas, alongside President Trump and Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega, both 80.
In a speech to ecstatic supporters in São Paulo, Lula said the election was a "defeat of denialism. A defeat of lies."

"I want to thank the Brazilian people for this generosity they have shown me for so long, to thank the youth who took to the streets to defend democracy, and the elders who went to vote," Lula told the crowd.
Lula's victory bucks a broader rightward shift across Latin America in recent years. In a pointed message to Trump, Lula declared that Brazil would not accept being "anyone's backyard."

Election day unfolded chaotically. Around midday, Lula's campaign requested an extension of voting hours, arguing that some local governments had reduced bus services, making it harder for voters to reach polling stations. Bolsonaro also sought an extension, citing heavy rain in some states.
Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin extended voting by two hours, to 7 p.m., but some polling stations had already deactivated their electronic voting machines and could not resume voting.

Speaking briefly to journalists outside his home in Brasilia, Bolsonaro called the result "inexplicable" and said he would seek to annul the vote. "I will not give up on my Brazil, and I hope you won't give up either," he said.

Bolsonaro, 45, had campaigned on closer ties with President Trump and pledged to pardon his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for plotting a coup to overturn his 2022 election defeat to Lula.

Brazilians showed little enthusiasm for street campaigning in the early months. But Bolsonaro's first-round finish on Oct. 4 energized the contest, and in recent days supporters of both candidates have filled rallies and flooded social media in an effort to sway voters.
In the end, Lula's message of continuity and a focus on social spending prevailed.

"I think people woke up about the risk of a Bolsonaro government after the first round, and the mobilization made a difference," said Alessandra Miguel, a 35-year-old spa worker who voted for Lula in Rocinha, a favela in Rio de Janeiro.

Lula rose to national prominence as the leader of a metalworkers' union that organized strikes that helped bring down Brazil's dictatorship in the 1980s. Unions and progressive Catholic activists joined forces at the time to form the Workers' Party, which Lula has now represented in seven presidential elections.

During Lula's first two terms in office, from 2003 to 2010, Brazil's economy boomed, and millions of Brazilians rose out of poverty. But many voters turned their backs on the party when Lula and other leaders became embroiled in corruption scandals in the 2010s. Lula himself was jailed, though his convictions were later overturned on procedural grounds.

On foreign policy, Lula has worked to boost the political influence of countries in the Global South as a founding member of the BRICS group, a grouping of major emerging economies that includes Brazil, China, Russia, India and South Africa. He has argued that Brazil should maintain friendly relations with all major world powers, though his ties with China and Russia have sometimes led him to clash with Washington.

Lula's approval rating rose after he stood up to Trump, but his disapproval rating remained higher than his approval rating at the start of the election season. Brazil's economic growth has been slower than during Lula's first two terms, and many Brazilians felt he had not done enough to address crime and public security.
During the campaign, Lula sought to address those concerns by proposing a ban on sports betting, announcing a debt renegotiation program and backing tougher penalties for minors who commit crimes.

He will govern a sharply divided country. Brazilian political scientist Jairo Nicolau, who studies presidential elections, said one of the most striking features of this year's contest was the rigidity of Brazilians' political allegiances.
Unlike in past years, Nicolau said, "people's identity of belonging to a tribe became more important than how they view different policy options."

A United States appeals court has expressed doubt over the Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California, which seeks to force the state to throw out mail-in ballots it has deemed likely to go to non-citizens.
Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said on Sunday that the three-judge panel would issue a decision as soon as possible, following a rare weekend oral argument.
But Bennett, an appointee of Republican President Donald Trump, voiced concern that the lawsuit would not hold up to scrutiny.
He pointed to the Elections Clause in the US Constitution, which allows states — not the federal government — to administer elections.

“It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause,” Bennett told Justice Department lawyer Matthew Donnelly. “How can we do that?”
The case is part of a larger effort under the right-wing Trump administration to crack down on alleged non-citizen voting ahead of the crucial November 3 midterm elections.
On October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm races, the Justice Department issued a complaint targeting California, a left-wing stronghold.
It asked the federal court system to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots that the government says were sent to “likely non-citizens”.
The lawsuit indicates the Trump administration sent California officials a list of 20,000 names it believes are not eligible to vote, based on citizenship.
Trump has often pushed the discredited claim that the Democratic Party is benefiting from widespread voting by non-citizens.
California has long been one of the targets for his election misinformation.
Earlier this year, Trump denounced the state’s primaries after right-wing candidates like Los Angeles mayoral hopeful Spencer Pratt felt short of his expectations.
“There’s BIG cheating by the Dumocrats in California,” he wrote on social media at the time.
He then announced that the state would be under investigation from the US attorney’s office.
Trump’s efforts have caused alarm, with critics accusing him of seeking to dampen voter turnout through intimidation and confusion.
The midterms will decide which party controls the US Congress, as well as key state and local positions.
Polls, however, predict steep odds for Republican candidates, given Trump’s souring approval ratings and dissatisfaction with issues like the cost of living and the US-Israeli war against Iran.

Voting rights advocates have warned that the Trump administration has not publicly revealed how it has compiled its list of non-citizen voters, and whistleblower reports have cast doubt on the accuracy of such lists.
In response to the October 15 lawsuit, California has countered that it has strong safeguards to prevent non-citizens from voting.
It also said that the Justice Department’s claims are based on dubious data.

“This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day,” California Governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement earlier this month.
“We will continue to carry out free and fair elections in the Golden State — and call out this authoritarian as he tries every play in the dictator’s playbook.”

A nurse has been killed and another health worker severely injured after they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), according to the World Health Organization.
It was the latest in a series of attacks on health workers and responders that authorities say is hampering efforts to slow the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in the world.
The attack took place on Saturday in the town of Bafwasende in the DRC’s eastern Tshopo province, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a post on X on Sunday.
“Everyone working to protect communities from this deadly disease must be able to work in dignity and safety. Healthcare must always be protected,” he said.
The WHO’s regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, also condemned the attack on X.
“Health is NOT a target,” he said. “Those responding to the Ebola outbreak must be protected. Misinformation and fear must never fuel violence.”
Local authorities have not yet commented on the attack or the suspects.

Data from the DRC’s Ministry of Health indicate that more than 9,800 cases, including more than 4,700 deaths, have been recorded since the start of the outbreak in May, making it the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country’s history.
The government’s handling of the outbreak, combined with chronic corruption, has sown widespread distrust, with some even dismissing Ebola as a hoax.

Responders say scepticism about the disease among communities has complicated their efforts, including in remote areas and emerging hotspots already facing shortages of medical supplies and healthcare workers.

Last month, a DRC politician was beaten to death in North Kivu after publicly defending the government’s response to Ebola. He had called on the public to obey response measures, particularly social distancing and hand-washing, on a radio show.
In May, at the start of the outbreak, angry residents set alight two tents at health centres in two separate attacks in just one week.
Responders say some residents have held captive or threatened team members in designated health zones.
The current outbreak has now been reported in four countries across eastern, central and western Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
On Sunday, Uganda’s Minister of Health Chris Baryomunsi announced that all citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to the DRC will be quarantined for 21 days.

Uganda says it is Ebola-free after declaring an end to its latest outbreak in July. But health experts remain on alert after two people who had recently passed through the country later tested positive in Kenya and Nigeria.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people.
The strain responsible for the current outbreak, known as Bundibugyo, has no approved vaccine or specific treatment.

Symptoms can take up to 21 days to appear, according to the WHO. In an October 23 update, it urged stronger monitoring and cooperation across borders, while advising against restrictions on travel or trade with affected countries.

US military forces have helped Gulf countries export more than 1.5 billion barrels of oil since June, despite Iran’s efforts to control the critical waterway, according to US Central Command (COMMAND).
The US military command said on Sunday that more than 3,000 commercial vessels had transited the Strait of Hormuz with its support over the past six months.

It added that more than 95 percent of ships navigating the channel had sailed through safely in recent months despite Iranian threats, “clearly demonstrating that the United States and regional partners control the international waterway”.

CENTCOM announced the figures as Commander Admiral Brad Cooper made a visit to the region, during which he observed the “current operational environment” in the strait while flying in a US Army helicopter.
“We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry,” Cooper said in a statement.
“This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.”
Cooper said the primary transit routes for vessels in the strait were free of Iranian mines due to the “incredible efforts” of personnel who conduct mine clearance operations.
“We remain intensely focused on keeping commercial traffic flowing as we work with our teammates in the US interagency, Gulf Cooperation Council, and shipping industry,” he said.

Crude oil flows have largely returned to levels seen before the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in late February, despite the ongoing threat of attacks on commercial vessels by Iranian forces.
At least 16.5 million barrels of oil per day left the region in September, equal to the pre-war average, excluding Iran, according to market intelligence firm Kpler.
Analysts have attributed the rebound to a combination of offshore ship-to-ship transfers, US military escorts, and increased use of oil pipelines.
However, oil prices remain far higher than before the start of the war.
Brent crude futures stood at about $114.50 a barrel on Sunday, after easing about 2 percent from last week’s nearly six-month high.
Brent settled at $72.48 per barrel on February 27, the day before the US and Israel began strikes on Iran.

The first confirmed Ebola patients in Kenya and Nigeria may have crossed paths at Uganda's Entebbe International Airport, according to African health officials, as new information from Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account of the Nigerian patient's travel history.
Uganda, a country reporting no active Ebola infections, has become a focus of investigations into cases thousands of kilometers apart.

Uganda insists that it has no confirmed active cases of the deadly virus. Yet health authorities in Kenya and Nigeria are investigating Ebola infections involving people whose travel histories or contacts are connected to the East African nation.

Both patients passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, according to Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).
Health officials say the two may have crossed paths, although it has not been established whether they encountered each other or whether any transmission occurred at the airport.

The differing accounts have raised questions about whether Uganda was simply a transit point for infected travelers. Or could infections be going undetected along some of Africa's busiest cross-border routes?
The latest developments come after Switzerland disputed claims that the Nigerian patient had visited the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where an Ebola outbreak is underway.
Did the two Ebola patients cross paths in Uganda?
Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate confirmed an Ebola case in the capital, Abuja, involving a woman who had recently traveled to East Africa, including Uganda.
"Today we are confirming that there has been one imported case of Ebola virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory," Pate said.
The woman developed symptoms on October 7 and visited a private health facility on October 11. Further laboratory testing confirmed Ebola, and she was subsequently isolated for treatment.
Pate said the patient was stable and health officials had identified 44 contacts, including health care workers, caregivers, patients and people who may have encountered her during her travels.
But the woman's journey has become central to the investigation.

Speaking on Thursday, Mankoula said the first confirmed patients in Kenya and Nigeria were both known to have traveled through Entebbe International Airport on October 3. Investigators are examining whether the two patients were at the airport at the same time and whether their movements overlapped.
Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account
Uganda's Health Ministry says preliminary findings indicate that the Nigerian patient traveled to eastern DRCfor business before passing through Uganda without symptoms and returning to Nigeria.
"Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation," the ministry said in an October 20 statement.
But, on Friday, Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs directly disputed the account.
"She and her husband did not travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo," the department said in a statement to Reuters news agency.
The woman, identified by Swiss authorities as a Swiss national of Ugandan origin, is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja.

On Thursday, the Swiss government told Reuters that she was believed to have contracted Ebola while traveling with her husband in Uganda, although that assessment has not been independently confirmed.
The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa CDC also said Thursday that they had not received confirmed information establishing that the woman had traveled to the DRC.

The conflicting accounts raise fresh questions about where the woman was exposed to the virus and how accurately her movements were initially reconstructed. They do not, however, establish that she contracted Ebola in Uganda.
Uganda maintains that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says it is awaiting more detailed information from Nigeria about the woman's movements.
Kenya's missing contact complicates investigation

In Kenya, Uganda has emerged in a separate investigation involving the country's first confirmed Ebola patient, who died in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, on October 5. The patient had traveled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before reaching Kenya.

Health officials have now established that the patient passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, the same day as the woman subsequently diagnosed in Nigeria. Kenyan authorities have since reported additional infections linked to the initial case.
But one aspect of the investigation remains unresolved.
According to Kenya's Daily Nation, health officials are searching for a Ugandan national identified as a contact of the deceased patient.
"We know him (the Ugandan) by name and passport number and from his phone but we are not able to reach him," Kenya's director-general for health, Patrick Amoth, told the newspaper.
The Daily Nation reported that the man was using a South Sudanese telephone number, complicating efforts to establish his whereabouts.
Being an untraced contact does not mean that he is infected. However, locating potentially exposed individuals is essential to preventing further transmission.
Uganda shares a lengthy border with the Democratic Republic of Congo, where Ebola outbreaks have repeatedly challenged health authorities.
Cross-border trade, population movements and international travel make it difficult to establish where someone was exposed to the virus.
Ebola symptoms typically develop two to 21 days after infection. According to the WHO, people infected with Ebola are not considered infectious until symptoms appear.
Even well-functioning border surveillance systems cannot identify every infected traveler.

The discovery that both patients traveled through the same international airport on the same day illustrates the complexity of tracing potential exposures across multiple countries. It also highlights the importance of reconstructing travel histories and identifying close contacts.
Uganda says it is strengthening screening and public health controls at points of entry. Nigeria has intensified contact tracing and infection prevention measures.
The challenge is ensuring that authorities across different countries can exchange accurate information quickly enough to identify potential exposures.

In Abuja, the confirmed infection has revived memories of previous Ebola outbreaks. Resident Peace Kolawole expressed concern about the consequences of another outbreak. "So here is my hand sanitizer, so I'm actually very concerned about it," she told DW.

Others fear that Nigeria's health care system may struggle to respond while many citizens face economic hardship. "Because now people are not even worried about sickness anymore, people are worried about surviving," Abuja resident Jonathan Steven told DW.
Nigeria's health authorities say the patient is receiving medical care and contact tracing is continuing.
Uganda's position between the DRC and other regional destinations offers one explanation for its appearance in both investigations.

But the latest findings have added two significant questions: Did the patients from Kenya and Nigeria come into contact at Entebbe International Airport on October 3? And where did the Nigerian woman contract the virus if, as Switzerland insists, she never traveled to DR Congo?

The conflicting accounts from Uganda and Switzerland have made establishing the Nigerian patient's travel history an urgent part of the investigation. The WHO and Africa CDC have yet to confirm the disputed DR Congo travel history.
Uganda's declaration of zero confirmed active cases does not establish that all infections have been ruled out. Equally, the travel histories do not prove an undetected outbreak.

For Kenya and Nigeria, the immediate priority is containing confirmed infections. For Uganda, the challenge is demonstrating that its surveillance systems are effective and reassuring both its citizens and neighboring countries.
The Africa CDC will convene an "extraordinary virtual meeting" of national health officials on October 28 as the continent's latest Ebola outbreak continues to spread.
Under attack from the militant Houthi group in neighboring Yemen, Saudi Arabia has asked numerous allies for help.
That includes the United States, even though media report that US President Donald Trump refused when Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman asked him to take direct military action against the Houthis.

However the US is providing Saudi Arabia with intelligence, which includes a targeting tool that uses artificial intelligence, or AI. A September report by US broadcaster CNN, quoting several unnamed American officials, said that between 100 and 200 US soldiers were in Saudi Arabia as part of new joint force command to facilitate this.
The US personnel were helping the Saudis "use a targeting tool that allows military officers to see in real-time what is happening on the battlefield," CNN reported.
Officials said the system in Saudi Arabia was similar to that known as the Maven Smart System, or MSS for short, which the US military has also used as it sought targets in Iran, Iraq and Syria.

MSS came out of what's known as Project Maven, the US's flagship artificial intelligence program for the military, first launched in 2017. MSS itself is an AI-enabled digital platform that "aggregates, organizes and visualizes vast streams of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance data," analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington explained in a June text.

The software system identifies patterns in data coming from, for example, live satellite feeds or drone cameras and then labels potential targets such as possible rocket launchers, tanks or suspicious vehicle convoys.

Previously human military analysts would have had to look at a wide array of different sources to try to find those, the CSIS researchers wrote. It was difficult and, in the case of hours of satellite or drone footage, almost impossible. But MSS now brings hundreds of sources together, analyses them all, then flags possible targets. It also calculates the best method of hitting the target.
Tech commentator Bilawal Sidhu, a former Google product manager, has described the MSS set up as like a "Google Earth for war."
Using the MSS dramatically speeds up what is known as "the kill chain" — that is, the time it takes to detect a target, decide if it's dangerous and then order a strike.

When the US military used MSS while attacking Iran in late February, the AI-powered system facilitated hits on more than 1,000 targets within the first 24 hours of the war. Previously American soldiers were hitting about 100 targets a day.
Up until recently, the long-simmering civil war in Yemen had been comparatively calm following an informal ceasefire negotiated in 2022.

The Houthi rebel group has held large parts of northern and western Yemen since 2015. Yemen's internationally recognized government and other groups held territory across the south and east. That latter is supported by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

The Houthi's latest military campaign, which began in September, has seen the group take further control of Yemen's coast. They also ramped up attacks against Saudi Arabia again, hitting the country's main airport and oil facilities. So far, though, military campaigns against the Houthi group by Saudi Arabia, the United States and others have all failed to significantly weaken the group.

This is partially because the Houthis take a "zero-sum approach," Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow focused on Yemen at UK think tank Chatham House, told DW recently. The group's founding father argued that contemporary Muslim societies were too "soft," and that poverty and hardship are a divine test, al-Muslimi said.
"They don't care if the Israelis bomb the airport or the US bombs a hospital," the expert said. "It actually serves them very well because their ideology is all about martyrdom and sacrifice."
There are certain technical issues users have noted with the MSS in the past that could also prove problematic in Yemen.

The Houthis tend to be highly mobile, using truck-mounted ballistic missiles and small drone swarms as they operate from hills and canyons in rugged countryside. It's possible that fighters might be long gone before they can be attacked even with the help of AI-assisted targeting.

Though MSS is known to work best in relatively unpopulated areas, factors such as changes in desert terrain, dust storms, high wind, snowfall and dense foliage — and even deliberately planted decoys — can reduce its success rate.
There is also a worrying ethical aspect to shortening the kill chain. A human is always supposed to verify the target that the AI-assisted tool has identified and decide how to react.

But it doesn't always work that way. For example, among the sites MSS targeted in Iran on the first day of the war was a school. An American missile killed almost 200 people at a primary school in southern Iran, most of them children aged between seven and 12.

In its military campaign in Gaza, Israel — arguably the Middle Eastern country with the most advanced military-use AI — has also used AI-assisted targeting. An Israeli system known as the Gospel, or Habsora, is the closest to MSS in the way it works.

But, as has been documented elsewhere, including by Israeli and British journalists and in the recent documentary Naza, the use of such AI targeting tools have also been highly problematic because of the numbers of civilian casualties that can result.

"On the one hand [in Gaza], AI has enhanced commanders' situational awareness, lessened the human costs of tunnel mapping, improved the speed of military strikes, and boosted the survivability of troops," analysts Frederic Wehrey and Andrew Bonney wrote for War on the Rocks, a specialist media outlet. "Yet the benefits afforded by such functions have been overshadowed by mounting civilian deaths reportedly resulting from this technology's safeguards being loosened or eliminated."

All of which is why Antony Loewenstein, an independent journalist based in Australia who has researched the impact of Israel's AI-assisted technology, doesn't believe similar technology will lead to the defeat of the Houthi group.

"I don't think there's much evidence at all that using an AI tool is going to make much difference on the ground, except for causing huge amounts of civilian casualties," Loewenstein, who authored the book, "The Palestine Laboratory: How Israel Exports The Technology of Occupation Around the World," told DW. "And I think what the US and the Saudis will find is that the Houthis have an incredibly high tolerance level for destruction."
Record low turnout in Sunday's Bulgarian elections mean voters are expected to head to the polls on November 1 to cast ballots in a presidential run-off.
Polling stations opened at 7 a.m. and closed at 8 p.m. (0500-1800 GMT), with official results expected within 48 hours, but voter turnout was less than 40%, far short of the 50% required.

Voters were choosing between candidates with vastly different views of the war in Ukraine and relations with Moscow and the vote came as drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea off the Bulgarian coast brought home the significance of the conflict in Ukraine for the former Soviet satellite state.

Although the presidency is largely ceremonial, the head of state in Bulgaria can appoint interim governments during political crises, is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and is able to veto legislation.
Who are the main candidates in Bulgaria's presidential election?

Frontrunner in the elections is incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who took over the position this year after current Prime Minister Rumen Radev stepped down to take part in the parliamentary elections that led him to power.
Yotova, 62, who surveys show as having 41-47% of the vote, favors dialogue with Moscow as the way to bring peace to Ukraine and opposes military aid to Kyiv.
A win for Yotova would give a boost for Radev, who also advocates dialogue with Moscow. Victory would make Yotova Bulgaria’s first elected female president.
Her main challenger is Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister, who is polling at 28-31%.

Gyurov, 50, who is backed by the pro-Western opposition, is an outspoken critic of Radev's foreign policy and strongly supports the Euro-Atlantic ties of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member state. As caretaker prime minister, Gyurov signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv.
The leader of the pro-Russian far-right Vazrazhdane party, Kostadin Kostadinov, is in third place on 10-13%.
Altogether 27 pairs of candidates for president and vice president are competing in the first round, with nearly half of them openly pro-Kremlin.

After casting her ballot in Sofia, Yotova called for peace, stability and unity, urging an end to divisions among Bulgarians. Her main challenger, Gyurov, voted in Blagoevgrad, calling for a Bulgaria that looks ahead and offers families greater economic security.
Turnout was estimated at 15.1% by 3 p.m. local time (1300 GMT), according to polling agency Myara, Bulgarian media reported.
To win outright, a candidate must secure more than half the valid votes, with more than half of eligible voters taking part. Otherwise, the top two candidates advance to a runoff on November 1.
What are the main issues in Bulgaria's presidential election?

The war in Ukraine triggered by Russia's unprovoked invasion is one of the central themes in the election, particularly after four merchant ships were allegedly hit by drones off Bulgaria's coast this month in suspected spillover from the conflict. The attacks have prompted Bulgaria to seek assistance from its allies to strengthen maritime security.
Satellite internet antennas from the Starlink network — an important part of Ukraine's defense capabilities — were also set on fire near the capital, Sofia.
While Radev has said that the attacks seemed to be to the advantage of Russia and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government has declined to blame the incidents directly on Moscow.
The strikes have nonetheless raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict.
Rising energy prices and inflation that have caused economic hardship to many in Bulgaria, the EU's poorest member state, are also a main issue addressed by candidates.
Many voters are also looking to stop government corruption, a persistent concern in the country, and hope for a stable government after multiple elections and coalition breakdowns in recent years.
