Lula re-elected in Brazil as Bolsonaro rejects results
Result keeps some distance between Latin America's biggest economy and Washington

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of U.S. President Donald Trump, was re-elected on Sunday in a result that keeps some distance between Latin America's biggest economy and Washington.

With 100 per cent of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes — 51.8 per cent of the total vote — over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro.
The announcement capped an evening of chaos at polling places across Brazil, following a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours.

Late Sunday, Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat, calling the move to extend voting hours unprecedented — though both he and Lula made the request — and asked for the election results to be annulled, saying they were impossible to accept.
In addressing supporters, Lula expressed his gratitude to the Brazilian people and pledged to respect all Brazilians, regardless of gender or religion. He also attacked Bolsonaro.
Lula supporters celebrate election results in Sao Paulo on Sunday. (Amanda Perobelli/Reuters)
"This was a defeat for denialism and lies. I must confess that every time I attended a debate, I felt embarrassed," he said.
Lula also doubled down on his commitment to Brazil's sovereignty.
"Either the homeland remains free or we die for Brazil," he said. "This country will not accept being anyone's backyard."

Lula's triumph bucks a trend in Latin America where increasing numbers of right-of-centre presidential candidates allied with Trump have been winning, further extending the United States' influence in the region.

His victory leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America's two most populous nations, with left-of-centre leaders. It also positions the region's largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion US per year, to remain independent of the U.S., despite the pressure of increased tariffs imposed by Trump.

A video published by Lula's campaign shows the veteran leader celebrating with his wife, Rosângela Lula da Silva, and allies after his run-off victory was confirmed by Brazil's electoral court. Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife. Hundreds of his supporters began gathering on São Paulo's main artery to celebrate the victory.

In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the colour of Lula supporters — shouted "You lost! Cry harder!" to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colours. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.
Lula's supporters celebrate in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday. (Lucas Landau/The Associated Press)

Rodrigo Valentim, a 51-year-old businessman and supporter of Bolsonaro, said that another Lula government would harm the economy. He pointed to financial markets' positive reaction to the result of the first round, when Bolsonaro bested Lula.
"I don't understand how people can vote for Lula," he said. "The country is collapsing."

The electoral court's announcement ended an evening of confusion at polling places after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled three minutes before the scheduled end of voting to keep polls open for two more hours, following requests by both candidates.

Lula's request came after issues with buses that provide transportation to polls in São Paulo and Salvador, two cities that tend to favour the incumbent. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south, where he is favoured.

In Brasilia, volunteers who oversaw the vote count at a school debated whether they needed to stay after the announcement to extend voting, but most left 15 to 20 minutes after polls closed and they had given count information to electoral authorities.
People line up outside a polling station in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday. (Agustin Marcarian/Reuters)
At a polling station in Rio de Janeiro, the voting machines had already been switched off minutes after polls were set to close and couldn't be turned back on.
The decision delayed tallying the votes by two hours. It was unclear how many polling stations stayed open after the scheduled closing time.
Bolsonaro ally Nikolas Ferreira noted that Zanin, who made the decision, is Lula's former lawyer.
Cost of living, security top of mind for voters

Bolsonaro bested Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round of the election earlier this month. Sunday night's apparent victory by Lula marked the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency.

Lula faced a tough re-election battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to bring down food costs, while Lula, trying to lure undecided voters, has invested in costly incentives.
Presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro walks toward a voting booth at a polling station in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday. (Mauro Pimentel/AFP/Getty Images)

Both have been hit by corruption suspicions involving family members and allies, with Bolsonaro implicated in a sprawling scandal rocking Brazil. Lula previously spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled.

This will likely be the last victory of the veteran leader's political career. Lula began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He then helped found the Workers' Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won in 2002. He was re-elected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was re-elected in 2014.

Rousseff was impeached for accounting manoeuvring in 2016 amid a sprawling corruption probe, which also ensnared Lula. He tried to run for president again in 2018 but was jailed in March after being convicted.
Members of the military police stand guard as people gather to watch election results in São Paulo on Sunday. (Jean Carniel/Reuters)

Lula was released from prison after 580 days and saw Brazil's Supreme Court annul his sentence after police found messages that showed the judge who convicted him was biased. He quickly became one of former president Jair Bolsonaro's biggest critics and narrowly beat him in 2022.

Since he lost the first round, Lula reorganized his campaign, appealed to young voters, put millions of Brazilians on the streets to defend democratic values and his legacy, raised fears of another Bolsonaro administration and boosted several government initiatives.
He joins Trump and Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega — all aged 80 — as the oldest presidents in the Americas.
Serbia's longtime strongman Vučić concedes election defeat to student-led opposition
Streets of Belgrade erupted in celebration after ex-leader's announcement
Serbia's Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Sunday that ends his long grip on power and heralds a new political era in the Balkan country.
Vučić, a populist and nationalist, has dominated Serbian politics as prime minister or president since 2014.

But he called a snap election in September after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024.
"It is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won,' Vučić said in a televised speech.
Within moments of his announcement, the streets of the capital, Belgrade, erupted in celebration after Vučić's announcement, with cars honking and students shouting "victory" and "he's done."
The students' win marks a profound political shift in the country of some six million people and is reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary's Viktor Orbán in April.

It may also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest — in some cases violently — against poor education standards and a lack of prospects.
Vučić said the students would have between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament and that his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) will have 105, based on preliminary results.

"Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard," said Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. "Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future."

Lines of unprecedented length had snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country earlier in the day, and even Vučić waited for nearly two hours to vote in Belgrade. Pollsters and the election commission put turnout at close to 70 per cent, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.
"[The turnout] did not surprise me because there was a large and strong mass that has formed throughout the past two years," voter Katarina Petrovic said.
People line up outside a polling station in Belgrade on Sunday. (Armin Durgut/The Associated Press)
Vučić, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, was a strong incumbent, and few in the student protest movement dared believe that he would concede so fast.
Supporters credit him with modernizing Serbia's economy and building new highways, railways, schools and hospitals.
"Some businessmen, some people will leave us, but our structure is firm, we are very united, very strong, we are used to being in the opposition," Vučić said.
Much remains unclear about how the student-backed candidates will fare.

Their list of 250 largely unknown personalities includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, although it is still unclear who will be prime minister.

The students' domestic agenda aims to root out graft and improve schooling. Political analysts predict some kind of purge of Vučić allies in the police, security services and ministries. But the students have been quieter on their international ambitions.

As Vučić did for years, they will have to juggle relations with China, a major investor; Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas; and the European Union, Serbia's largest trading partner.

The student-led street protests, sparked by the station disaster, started small but quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vučić to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression has worsened in the period since.

"For decades the people have been waiting for this time, something to bring hope that we can live freely and by the rules of democracy," actor Jelena Stupljanin, 48, said at a Belgrade polling station.
A voter casts a ballot into a box at a polling station in Belgrade on Sunday. (Marko Djurica/Reuters)

Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He said the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss.

Meanwhile, on the streets of Belgrade, a traditional brass band struck up, and a group including a man in a "students are champions" jumper floated balloons in the shape of the number 3, representing the number of the students' list of candidates.
"We will drink a beer to celebrate, we will get drunk, we are so happy, I have no words to describe how much," said Andjela, a student who was with a group of friends.
Carney's geopolitical ambitions tested in defence industry co-operation with Turkey
Developing partnership allows Canada to lessen dependence on U.S. military suppliers

While in Istanbul this past week, Prime Minister Mark Carney struggled for a moment when asked to describe how he felt about limits that had been placed on Ukraine's access to the Starshield military-grade satellite network.
When he found his voice, he spoke about the "immense human suffering" of missile strikes on Kyiv and elsewhere.

"I search for the right adjective to describe whoever took this decision, or a group of people took this decision, against a country — and it's against a country that is literally fighting for the lives of its citizens against naked aggression."
Carney was, however, quick to turn it into an object lesson for Canadians who are skeptical of warming relations with authoritarian-leaning Turkey.

"We as Canadians do not want to be caught in a situation where we are reliant on one provider that may change their view, or may be forced to change their views, by one nation state that puts Canadians at risk — or compromises our sovereignty, our ability to express our values and live our values.”

Early last week, Ukrainian officials said they had lost some of their access to Starshield, the military version of Starlink, the global satellite communications system owned and operated by Elon Musk's company SpaceX.
Ukraine employs Starshield to both track incoming missiles and jet-powered drones, and to guide interceptor and spy drones, while using Starlink for critical internal communications.
Without mentioning the United States or the Trump administration, Carney's reference was clear: We don't want to find ourselves in the same situation as Ukraine.
Canadian officials have made no secret of wanting to reduce reliance on Starlink in favour of a future Telesat system.

Much of Carney’s recent whirlwind trip to Istanbul and the Turkish capital, Ankara, was framed through the lens of the contradiction of values-based Canadians cosying up to a regime that shuts down opposition television stations, arrests journalists and attacks 2SLGBTQ+ advocates.

What was mentioned as part of a strategic partnership signed by Carney — but received far less scrutiny — is the burgeoning defence-industrial co-operation between the two countries, which arguably is an early test of Carney's geopolitical ambitions.

"Canada-Turkey defence co-operation is an early test of whether the middle-power co-ordination the prime minister called for at Davos can produce anything more durable than a sequence of transactions,” wrote Tolga Demiryol, an associate professor of political science at Altınbaş University in Istanbul. He was referring to Carney's speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January.
A research paper penned by Demiryol was published on the Canadian Global Affairs Institute website in early October.
He said both countries now share a similar outlook when it comes to the defence industry as an instrument of national sovereignty.

"Canada is seeking to reduce the concentration of its defence procurement in the United States, while Turkey's industry was built through repeated efforts to escape foreign control over critical components and export permissions," Demiryol wrote.
"Turkey is courted today for two reasons: it has more to offer than it once did; and Canada has more reason than it once had to look beyond the United States."
Demiryol also said Carney is is not searching "for a replacement partner, but rather to reduce Canadian exposure to any single foreign supplier."
In addition to it being an early test of Carney's middle-power strategy, the defence partnership represents a leap of faith.
Not many years have passed since the events that sent relations between Canada and Turkey into the wilderness.
In 2020, Turkish authorities applied for an exemption related to the importation of target acquisition gear, made by Canadian company Wescam, used in Turkey's Bayraktar drones.
Documents made public stated that Turkish authorities claimed they were using the cameras for reconnaissance activities related to NATO operations in the north of Syria.
But it was later discovered that the cameras were illegally diverted to Azerbaijan and used during the war in Nagorno-Karabakh.
Human rights groups accused Turkey of lying to the Canadian government.
The de facto arms embargo that resulted was lifted in early 2024 when Canada's Department of Foreign Affairs stopped presumptively denying arms export permits to the Middle Eastern country.

While trust has been restored, Carney made clear following talks with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan that the agreement signed on Thursday does not mean unfettered exports and that permits will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.
"We have standards, we have rules and we will follow them, we will continue to follow them," Carney said.

So what's the attraction of Turkey's defence sector? The short answer is the country's capacity to go from reliance on foreign defence contractors to building its own equipment in a short period of time.

"An important point here, I believe that in Turkey, about 80 per cent of the defence needs of this country are produced here. This is not the case in Canada," Carney said. "So there are a lot of lessons for us on how we can create an industry in our country."
It is also the type of military equipment that Turkey is building that makes it attractive.
A Turkish TB2 drone is seen in Golcuk, Turkey, on Aug. 21. (Burak Kara/Getty Images)

Drones are one example. The TB2, manufactured by Baykar — a private defence and tech company that Carney met with during his stop in Istanbul — proved itself in combat during the opening phase of the war in Ukraine by stopping Russian armoured columns with deadly precision strikes. The country is now manufacturing land and sea drones. It is also developing its own next-generation fighter jet, known as KAAN.

Carney didn't rule out buying Turkish military equipment such as the TB2 but suggested the country's know-how and ability to integrate technologies will be important as Canada expands it own industry.
"We're in a position where we're more in need of Turkish expertise in terms of reinforcing what we need to do to protect Canadians and to serve as a full NATO ally at this stage," Carney said.
Mike Ward, executive director of the Canada Turkey Business Council, said direct investment is another attractive aspect for the prime minister.
Last year, four major Turkish defence companies visited the Toronto Global Forum and pitched investment in Canada's aerospace sector, among others.
"They said, 'Look, we want to do business with Canada. And sure ... Canadian companies can invest in Turkey if you'd like. But we really want to invest in Canada,'" Ward said.
"And those companies have been back. So they're looking to invest. They're looking to invest in Ontario. They're looking to invest to Quebec."
In Europe, Baykar finalized the purchase of an Italian aerospace company, Piaggio, in June 2025. It is also in joint partnership with that country's leading aircraft maker, Leonardo, to build drones.
Demiryol, of Altınbaş University, said he sees shared production and joint rights as a possible way ahead for Canada and Turkey in this new relationship.
But he said transparency will be key to making it work and avoiding the issues that led to the breakdown in relations.
After waiting years for specialist care through Canberra Health Services (CHS), some patients have found out they have been removed from waitlists via a letter in the mail.
CHS says it is "systematically working through" waitlists, and that the criteria for services like the paediatric allergy clinic had changed.
ACT Opposition Leader Mark Parton says he will move a motion this week calling on the government to "honour the original waiting lists".
When Liz Allen's daughter was seven years old, she suffered an anaphylactic response while helping to peel prawns for a Christmas meal.
She's since had allergic reactions to other unidentified allergens, some of which have involved trips to the emergency department.
In January 2024, Ms Allen said her daughter was referred to Canberra Health Services' paediatric allergy clinic because it was "the best, most comprehensive place" to determine what was going on.

But in mid-October, after almost three years of waiting, she received a letter stating that her daughter had been removed from the waitlist because her condition "no longer meets the requirement for a specialist appointment".
"It is stressful because … it could be life threatening," Ms Allen said.
"Not knowing the source of the allergy is of great concern.
"We have waited on this list patiently in the belief that she would get the medical treatment she needs."
Ms Allen said she received no other communication from Canberra Health Services (CHS) before the letter arrived.
"There was certainly no communication about further information, particularly around her [current] health," she said.
"Each new reaction [she has] occurs about every six months. It is getting more and more of a concern for us as she gets older."
The letter from CHS explained that there were more than 65,000 people on outpatient waiting lists, and that the wait for the allergy centre was more than six years long for some patients.
"To deliver an effective service, the criteria we use to decide which patients can be seen at the clinic has recently been reviewed and updated by our clinicians," the letter stated.

"Our team has reviewed the information your doctor sent us against the new criteria, and your referral no longer meets the criteria for a specialist appointment with CHS, and your referral has been closed."
Ms Allen said it was a "kick in the guts" to have to "start all over again", particularly given their referring doctor had since retired.
"We feel like as family, we are in nowhere land trying to navigate this issue," she said.
A post on social media about her experience attracted dozens of comments from other Canberrans who had received similar letters.
"How is it that the criteria has changed so that even an anaphylactic … response does not make a child eligible for such a service?," she said.
"I do worry about this whole system that appears to be crumbling.
"And that doesn't bode well for families trying to raise healthy children."
CHS 'systematically working through' wait lists

CHS chief operating officer Alison Derritt told 666 ABC Canberra Breakfast that they were "systematically working through" more than 40 outpatient waiting lists as part of a review of specialist and outpatient services.
"There will be more reviews to occur. We are working service by service," she said.
"We need to work through all 40-odd services to understand their waitlists and go through them."
She said the current criteria for the paediatric allergy service was "those under 16 with a severe and complex food allergy, and primarily with the history of anaphylaxis".
"Now we do need to talk to [Liz Allen] ... and certainly happy to understand her particular situation," she said.
"But what we're trying to do is focus on those patients that are at the top categories or top of the new categories and be able to see them in a timely way."
Ms Derritt said that some patients removed from waitlists would need to look at being "seen elsewhere", and one "alternate" would be to go to a private clinic.
She also said some patients needing a "lower category service" may be able to access other local services without needing to travel interstate.

"If someone has got communication or a letter from us and you consider that we've not fully appreciated the situation or there's additional information that you think that we've missed, we're very happy to talk through that with our patients and families," she said.
'Honour original waiting lists': Opposition
ACT Opposition Leader Mark Parton has criticised CHS's process, and accused the government of trying to make waitlists look better.
"We understand that they're going through a process of review, but we don't believe that process of review should mean weeding out everyone on the waiting list and starting from scratch,"
Mr Parton said he would move a motion in the ACT Legislative Assembly this week, calling on the government to "honour the original waiting lists".
"It doesn't matter which way you look at this situation, it's diabolically bad," he said.
"I don't know how the government's going to defend its position because I think it's indefensible.
"And I would hope that the motion that I run tomorrow will give the government the ability to walk back from this and actually genuinely look after the people who need looking after."

Robert John Crawford is accused of murdering his wife Frances Crawford at their home in 2024 and staging it as an accident.
The Brisbane Supreme Court heard the former RAAF pilot loved money so much "he killed for it".
Mr Crawford has pleaded not guilty to domestic violence murder.
A former RAAF pilot accused of murdering his wife at their Queensland home embarked on a "campaign to make her death appear like a tragic accident", the Brisbane Supreme Court has heard.

On the first day of Robert John Crawford's trial for the alleged murder of his wife Frances Crawford, the court heard he was a "master manipulator", "adulterer and philanderer" who loved money so much he "killed for it".
The former RAAF squadron leader is accused of strangling his wife, and or causing blunt force trauma to her head at their Upper Lockyer home in late July 2024.
The Crown alleged Mr Crawford then manipulated the scene to try and make it appear like she fell while moving their ride-on mower one evening.
On Monday, the court was shown a photo of the mother-of-three's body where it was found beside the mower, which was tipped on its side, next to a retaining wall at their semi-rural property.
According to the prosecution, a "perfect storm" was brewing in the lead up to the alleged murder.
The prosecution said this meant Mr Crawford was due to lose out financially in a divorce settlement, prompted by his infidelity over many years.
"Mr Crawford was interested in other women and not committed to his marriage,"
"He wanted to retain possession and occupancy of their house at Upper Lockyer."

He said Mr Crawford had not wanted to split his lucrative superannuation with his wife in any settlement, and did not like conditions imposed on him during a period the couple were separated and attending counselling, while seeing if they could reconcile the marriage.
The week after Frances Crawford's alleged murder, her husband was due to undergo a "looming" polygraph test and was about to be "booted" out of the couples $2.6 million home, the court heard.
Mr Crawford has pleaded not guilty to one charge of domestic violence murder.
He has been on bail for more than two years as he awaited the trial, which is set down to run for about three weeks.

The jury heard the Crown planned to call nearly 50 witnesses, including the couple's children, Frances Crawford's siblings and friends, first responders, and various forensic, DNA and ecological experts.
A number of Mr Crawford's former RAAF colleagues, and the women he allegedly had relationships and affairs with in the years before his wife's death are also expected to give evidence.
Before her alleged murder in 2024, Frances Crawford worked part time as a psychologist in Toowoomba.
The court heard that she was a devout Christian, and despite wanting "to be loved by her husband" and "live happily ever after like a fairy tale", she instead felt "unsafe" in her marriage.
A number of her loved ones attended court for the first day of the trial, with some to speak as witnesses, while others sat in the public gallery in support of the mother-of-three.

PARIS — American football fans brought high energy, chants and smiles to Stade de France on Sunday to watch the Pittsburgh Steelers face the New Orleans Saints. Some said the mass protests in the city were not an issue during their weekend trip.

The NFL’s first regular-season game in France came a day after more than 400,000 people around the country took to the streets to protest educational funding and the high cost of living. At least 110,000 of those protesters were concentrated in Paris, according to the French Interior Ministry.

Although the demonstrations were largely peaceful, some clashes broke out, prompting French security forces to use tear gas and water cannons in several cities. Paris prosecutors said there were 64 arrests in the nation’s capital on Saturday, mostly for suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage.
But American visitors in town to cheer on their teams told NBC News that everyone they’ve encountered had been welcoming.

Lifelong friends and Saints fans Sindhu Pandit, Shruti Menon and Pramod Menon said they never felt the game would be canceled. Pandit said the key to their own movements around the city was to stay informed.

Pramod Menon added that locals were “incredibly hospitable” and considerate of the fact that they were visitors. The friends said they came to support both the country and their team, a sentiment his wife shared.
“We’re so excited to be here in Paris, and what a perfect place for New Orleans, the home of the French,” Shruti Menon said. “And so it’s wonderful to be here.”
Sean Warner, a Steelers fan since 1974, may not share the Menons’ taste in teams, but he also told NBC News that he and his wife, Saroja, were having a “wonderful” time in Paris.

“We were concerned about the riots and everything that we had heard about and read about, but quite honestly, it’s been amazing,” he said. “The experience has been fantastic. ... Paris has really tried to work hard to, you know, make people feel safe and comfortable, and then enjoy the experience.”

The Washington, D.C.-based couple, who have visited Paris several times, spent Saturday walking around the city. Saroja Warner said it was a bit sad to see some businesses with boarded-up windows, but any clashes seemed “localized.”

“We walked around Paris all day till about 6 o’clock at night ... and we didn’t see any unrest, any crazy stuff,” she said. “It just felt like a lot of folks trying to have a nice time on a rainy day in Paris.”

The Steelers beat the Saints 16-10 at France’s national stadium, just outside the heart of Paris. The game is the latest in a series of international games the NFL has scheduled in recent seasons to grow the sport outside of its domestic audience.

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell told reporters Wednesday that he was not concerned about the Paris protests ahead of the game and was comfortable with the security preparations the league had made in coordination with French authorities.
“Protests are not unusual in France, as you know, and that’s something that we will be aware of and make sure that the appropriate arrangements are made,” Goodell said.

Figures from the Interior Ministry indicate Saturday’s demonstrations produced significantly fewer problems than those the week before. There were about 1,300 arrests nationwide, roughly half the previous week’s total. Only 53 members of the security forces reported injuries, compared with 1,144 the week before, according to the ministry.

The unrest began weeks ago, when students at a high school in Créteil, a suburb of Paris, began protesting a lack of resources and poor conditions at their school. Students at other schools in the poorer suburbs surrounding Paris soon joined, and the protests grew into a movement of students across France.

The teenagers blocked entrances to their schools and demanded that the French government invest in their educations by increasing staffing, repairing aging buildings and providing more resources to the public education system. Their protests caught the attention of many across the country who were struggling with the high cost of living.

Protest organizers agreed to the plans coordinated with the French government on Saturday, the Interior Ministry said Sunday. But the ministry warned that high-risk groups, largely made up “of radical far-left and ultraleft activists,” had infiltrated demonstrations in medium- and large-sized cities. It blamed those groups for “fomenting attacks” against law enforcement, businesses and other people.

“While the level of violence from these radical elements was the same as last week, their attempted actions — which triggered systematic intervention by law enforcement in line with the clear instructions of the Minister of the Interior — were generally thwarted,” the ministry said.
Richard Engel and Marc Smith reported from Paris and Doha Madani from New York City.

Why do planes keep circling before landing? The UN has a plan to fix it

Air traffic delays cost billions and turn journeys into ordeals. Some countries are already proving that better coordination saves thousands of flying hours and cuts emissions – and the UN’s aviation agency wants the rest of the world to follow.
Most frequent flyers know the feeling: the plane begins its descent but, instead of heading for the runway, starts circling overhead.
It isn’t necessarily a fault or bad weather. Often, it is a holding pattern – a manoeuvre that keeps aircraft airborne until there is room for them to land.
It is one symptom of increasingly crowded skies, where a storm, an emergency or a closed route in one place can cause delays thousands of kilometres away.
The bill is enormous. In Europe alone, air traffic management delays cost an estimated $2.3 billion or more in 2025, according to EUROCONTROL, the continent’s air navigation body.
What if countries coordinated their flights the way a city synchronises its traffic lights?
That is the idea behind a push by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the UN agency that sets global aviation standards.
“If the traffic lights work independently, traffic becomes chaos and there are jams on every corner,” ICAO Secretary General Juan Carlos Salazar told UN News.
“If you get a green light on one street and are stopped at the next, the backlog builds immediately. The same happens with air traffic across the world’s airspace.”

The fix starts long before landing. If an airport knows it cannot take more aircraft for a while, it can coordinate with other airports to hold back departures, rather than leave planes circling overhead.
This approach, known as air traffic flow management, lets airlines, airports, controllers and weather services share information and make decisions together.

Several countries already use it, but the benefits are limited when national systems don’t talk to each other. After five days of talks in Montreal convened by ICAO, governments and industry backed a faster global rollout.
For passengers, that should mean earlier warning of cancellations and delays as well as quicker recovery when things go wrong.
“When people get to the airport, wait all day and nobody tells them anything, that creates huge problems,” Mr. Salazar said.
Disruption snowballs, he explained. A problem lasting an hour or a day knocks on to every flight scheduled after it and today’s system is slow to bounce back.
The gains are already measurable. In the Americas, collaborative trials supported by ICAO saved more than 265,000 minutes of flying time in 2026, about 4,400 hours, and over $38.9 million.
They also saved some 13,330 tonnes of fuel and avoided 42,160 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions, a contribution to the goal of net zero carbon emissions from international aviation by 2050.

In Europe, a EUROCONTROL programme anticipating weather and congestion avoided around 3.1 million minutes of delay between May and August 2026, saving an estimated $448 million and making the network 14 per cent more stable on the worst days.
Brazil and Colombia have run such systems for years, Mr. Salazar said, but largely at national level while international flights cross many countries’ airspace.
“Technology alone is not the answer,” he said. Information has to be shared and often it isn’t, sometimes for lack of will, sometimes for lack of the means to transmit it in real time.

“A flight from Europe to Australia or New Zealand passes through four or five regions, different continents and that requires excellent coordination which doesn’t exist today,” he said. “No country or region acting alone can manage that.”

ICAO, with 193 member States, sets common standards and provides technical help so countries can coordinate regardless of resources. New international rules on flow management are due in November 2030, with regional workshops planned for 2027.
The pressure is mounting. ICAO projects air travel could reach 12.4 billion passengers by 2050.

Other challenges are piling up. Conflicts force airlines to reroute around danger zones, creating new bottlenecks. Drones, air taxis, rocket launches and unplanned re-entries of objects from orbit all demand closer coordination.
For Mr. Salazar, the goal is simple: “an air transport system that reaches every person in the world, so that everyone sees the benefits of being connected.”

The Soil Mapping for Resilient Agrifood systems (SoilFER) programme supports farmers to develop reliable soil information that will inform agricultural decisions such as which fertilizer to use and how much.

“I want to urge Kenyans that before thinking about what to plant or the fertilizer to use, think about soil testing,” he said.
The event also marked the launch of the Kenya Soil Partnership, the Kenya Soil Laboratory Network and the national rollout of the Global Soil Doctors Programme.
The SoilFER programme is currently being implemented in six other countries: Ghana, Guatemala, Honduras, Mozambique, Tunisia and Zambia.
‘Burden and loss’ builds in DR Congo, as Kenya strengthens Ebola containment

“If we lift the foot off the pedal, the virus will resurge very quickly, will continue to spread to newly affected areas and pose a threat for the country, the region and the world at large,” warned Dr. Catherine Smallwood, World Health Organization (WHO) incident manager in the DRC.

The country remains the epicentre of an outbreak of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease that was officially declared in mid-May. It began in the volatile eastern region and has now spread to eight provinces, the latest being Nord-Ubangi in the northwest.
There have been 9,765 cases to date and nearly half – 4,727 – have died. Additionally, 30,000 contacts are being monitored each day over a three-week period.
A smaller outbreak in Uganda was officially declared over in August, while cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and France.

In the DRC, “we’re seeing an incredible permanent burden and loss of livelihoods in those families that are affected”, said Dr. Smallwood, speaking from the eastern city of Bunia to journalists in Geneva.

At nearly six months in, the outbreak “is occurring in an area that is geographically vast and moving into ever hard to reach locations and remote locations”, she noted. Some places can take several days to reach by boat or motorcycle and are inaccessible by car or plane.

The crisis continues to unfold amid ongoing conflict, hunger and displacement, and the World Food Programme (WFP) is working to ensure that families get enough to eat. The UN agency is also building Ebola treatment centres, among other operations.
WFP’s Representative in the DRC David Stevenson shared stories of the people who depend on its support.
One woman, Francine Birungi Amoti, lost a child to Ebola and is raising her six surviving children and a baby entrusted to her care. She is unable to attend to her fields due to violence.
“For Francine, food assistance means being able to feed the children in her care when reaching her fields could cost her life,” he said, speaking from the capital Kinshasa.
“This is what a crisis on top of a crisis looks like: disease and bereavement, compounded by insecurity and hunger.”
Dr. Smallwood also pointed to another concern as the number of people dying from Ebola outside recognised treatment centres “remains a big flag of late detection of cases at the community level”.

The past week has seen a decline in the number of people dying in the community or outside Ebola treatment centres which indicates that actions to increase early detection and quick referral to care have been working.

However, WHO understands that in some parts of eastern DRC, “patients are visiting between two to five different health facilities before they're referred to Ebola treatment centres”, representing “a really, really big challenge”.

Dr. Smallwood said there have been significant improvements in the quality of care provided at Ebola treatment centres. WHO had set a target of 3,000 beds across affected areas and currently over 2,000 are available.

She also highlighted the positive fact that 2,600 people in the DRC have survived Ebola. Clinics are being opened where they can access care, including to monitor presence of the virus and any related conditions that may arise, as well as psychosocial support.

There is also good news on the Ebola front in Kenya following the country’s first case and fatality earlier this month – a Kenyan man who had been working in the DRC before flying back to Nairobi via Uganda.
More than 100 contacts were identified, some of whom will complete their 21-day quarantine on Sunday and will be heading home to their families.
WHO representative in Kenya Dr. Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo welcomed the development.
“I think their sacrifice has been important in ensuring that the community is protected and that we don’t have community spread today,” she told UN News.
She stressed that these people should not be stigmatised as being released from quarantine does not mean that they had Ebola, only that they had contact with someone who did.
With Ebola now confirmed in four African countries, Dr. Kimambo underscored that governments must remain vigilant.

“Africa is very interconnected and nobody is safe until everyone is safe,” she said. “So, as long as we have Ebola in DRC at the scale that it is, or in any other country, it means that we are not safe. Therefore, the key message is preparedness.”

A simple liquid can stop cavities without drilling, major study confirms

- A simple liquid painted onto teeth in seconds can stop cavities without drilling, injections, or anesthesia, according to a major clinical trial involving young children. The inexpensive treatment could spare thousands of children painful dental procedures and surgery while paving the way for broader FDA-approved use.

A cavity doesn't always have to mean drilling, injections, or an uncomfortable visit to the dentist. A major clinical trial has confirmed that a simple, inexpensive liquid can stop tooth decay in young children, potentially preventing painful infections and the need for dental surgery.

The treatment, called silver diamine fluoride (SDF), takes only seconds to apply to each affected tooth. Rather than removing damaged tooth material and placing a filling, a dentist uses a tiny sponge tipped applicator to paint the liquid directly onto the cavity. The process requires no drilling, injections, or sedation.

The findings could have enormous implications for childhood dental care. Every year, thousands of young children in the United States visit emergency departments because of untreated cavities. Emergency physicians generally cannot provide the dental procedures needed to address the underlying problem, leaving some children with ongoing pain and infections. Others ultimately need dental surgery under general anesthesia, which makes them completely unconscious during the procedure.
Now, researchers led by the University of Michigan have produced compelling evidence that a much simpler approach can stop many cavities from getting worse.
Major Clinical Trial Confirms Silver Diamine Fluoride Works

Published in JAMA Pediatrics, the Phase III clinical trial included 830 children younger than 6. Participants were recruited through dental clinics, pediatric medical practices, and Head Start and Early Head Start programs in Michigan, New York, and Iowa.
Head Start and Early Head Start are federally supported programs that provide early childhood education and related services to eligible families.
The results showed that a solution containing 38% silver diamine fluoride successfully stopped decay in more than half of the affected baby teeth when treatment was provided at six month intervals.

Dentists refer to this as arresting tooth decay, meaning the damaged area stops deteriorating. Unlike a traditional filling, the treatment does not replace lost tooth structure. Instead, it helps prevent existing decay from progressing.

SDF works through the combined effects of silver and fluoride. Silver helps combat bacteria associated with tooth decay, while fluoride helps strengthen the mineral structure of teeth and resist further damage.

"This is a very effective and safe treatment -- even in children as young as 1," said Margherita Fontana, professor of dentistry at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry and the study's lead investigator.
A Simple Treatment Could Help Millions Avoid Dental Pain

Tooth decay is the most common chronic disease among children, affecting more than 40% of American children. Although cavities may initially cause few noticeable symptoms, untreated decay can eventually lead to severe toothaches, infections, problems eating and sleeping, missed school days, and repeated medical appointments.
For young children, conventional dental treatment can also be particularly challenging. Some are too young to remain still throughout a procedure, while others experience significant fear or anxiety.
SDF offers an alternative for many of these patients because it can be applied quickly without the equipment and procedures required for a traditional filling.

Fontana said the benefits could extend well beyond young children. Older adults, people with developmental or physical disabilities, individuals with severe dental anxiety, and patients who have difficulty obtaining conventional dental care could also benefit.

There is, however, one important tradeoff. SDF permanently turns the decayed portion of a treated tooth dark, which can be especially noticeable on front teeth. The discoloration is primarily cosmetic, but it may influence whether patients and families choose the treatment.
For many people, avoiding pain, drilling, or more invasive procedures may outweigh that drawback.
Why This Decades-Old Treatment Could Soon Reach More Patients
Silver diamine fluoride is not a newly invented substance. Dentists have successfully used it to manage cavities in numerous countries for decades.

In the United States, the FDA approved SDF as a medical device for treating tooth sensitivity in 2014. Dentists have also used it off-label to stop cavities, meaning they apply an authorized product for a purpose beyond its original approved indication.

What has been missing is large-scale clinical evidence from U.S. populations establishing its safety and effectiveness for treating tooth decay, a key step toward obtaining FDA approval for that specific use.
The University of Michigan trial was designed to help fill that gap.

"If we want more children and families to benefit from this treatment, we need rigorous evidence showing both that it works and that it's safe. From a public health perspective, if we want broader implementation across the United States, including in medical settings, we need carefully collected data in U.S. populations, and we now have that," Fontana said.
The investigation began in 2018 and continued despite the major disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The researchers believe stronger clinical evidence could make SDF more widely available, including in pediatric medical settings where children often receive care long before their first dental appointment.

"In medicine, clinicians want high-quality evidence before changing practice," Fontana said. "It is important to have data they can refer to because young children often see pediatricians years before they ever visit a dentist, broader acceptance could allow many more cavities to be treated while a referral to a dental home is successful, and before they become painful, infected or require surgery."
A dental home refers to an ongoing relationship with a dental care provider who can deliver preventive care, treatment, and follow-up services.
Expanding access to SDF could allow more children to receive early intervention before relatively manageable cavities develop into serious dental problems.
FDA Approval Could Expand Access to Cavity Treatment

The trial brought together researchers from the University of Michigan, New York University, the University of Iowa, and Indiana University. The National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, part of the National Institutes of Health, provided more than $12 million in funding.
The product tested was Advantage Arrest 38% SDF, supplied by Elevate Oral Care.
The findings provide clinical trial evidence that the manufacturer can use in an application seeking FDA approval of SDF as a drug for arresting dental caries, the medical term for tooth decay.
Amr Moursi, a professor of pediatric dentistry at New York University College of Dentistry and a co-principal investigator, emphasized the potential importance of that regulatory change.

"Our results support FDA approval of SDF for managing arrest of tooth decay in young children. Removing SDF from off-label status would be an important innovation which could lead to increased utilization by providers, enhanced payments by insurers and more consistent product quality," said Moursi, a co-principal investigator on the study.
For some children, receiving another application of SDF every few months could be sufficient to keep a cavity under control until the affected baby tooth naturally falls out.
Adults could also benefit, either by using SDF to manage decay over a longer period or as a temporary solution until a filling or another restorative procedure becomes affordable or practical.

The treatment is not suitable for every cavity, and stopping decay does not necessarily eliminate the need for future dental work. Nevertheless, the findings suggest that a procedure requiring only seconds to perform could help many patients avoid more complicated treatment.
"For almost anyone, this can arrest the decay and stop the infection and the pain it causes," Fontana said. "This could benefit many people."

Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

- Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.

Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."
Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.
Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%

The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.
Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.
According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."
A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors

The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."

The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

It's been 20 years since Australian researchers created the world's first vaccine developed specifically to prevent cancer.
Thanks to the HPV vaccine, Australia is on track to become one of the first nations in the world to eliminate cervical cancer.
Now, research led by scientists Down Under has made another breakthrough – this time for skin cancer.

The first personalized mRNA cancer vaccine has now succeeded in a phase 3 clinical trial, reducing the risk of melanoma returning or causing death by 42 percent compared with standard immunotherapy alone.
The results are even better than scientists were expecting.
The global principal investigator, medical oncologist Georgina Long from Melanoma Institute Australia (MIA), presented the results at the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress 2026.
They are set to be published in the New England Journal of Medicine.
"These findings are a foundational shift in our approach to cancer: harnessing the immune system in a more personalized way to reduce the risk of melanoma recurrence or death," says Long.
"This has not been achieved before in the history of cancer drug development."

Medical oncologist Robert Vonderheide, president-elect of the American Association for Cancer Research, who was not involved in the trial, told The New York Times the trial's results are up there with "our biggest breakthroughs."
The mRNA vaccine was developed by Moderna and Merck, and it is designed to stop melanoma from coming back after surgery.
First, researchers sequence the tumor from each patient, and then they figure out what separates the 'fingerprint' of this tumor from other, healthy cells in the body.
A vaccine based on that information essentially creates a personalized 'wanted poster' of the cancer for the patient's own immune system.
"This is delivered as mRNA, so the body's own cells display the poster to the immune system, showing it exactly what to look out for and attack," says Long.
The medicine works in conjunction with an existing immunotherapy called Keytruda (pembrolizumab).
"Cancer can fool the immune system with a fake friendly handshake, so the immune system thinks the cancer cell is normal," explains Long.
"Pembrolizumab blocks the handshake, allowing immune cells to recognize the cancer and attack it, but it is the same drug for everyone."
Personalizing a treatment to use alongside pembrolizumab seems to improve the results.
The phase 3 clinical trial involved more than 1,100 patients from 157 sites around the world, and the results back up impressive findings from a phase 2 trial, published in 2024.
For patients who remained cancer-free six months after starting treatment, the risk reduction for melanoma recurrence or death was 58 percent compared with pembrolizumab alone.
The mRNA vaccine is not yet available to patients in Australia or the United States, but the results have entered a regulatory review process.
That could take several years, depending on the nation.
In Australia, which has one of the highest melanoma rates in the world, one person dies from this cancer every 6 hours.
A vaccine that could stop the cancer from recurring could save numerous lives.
And it's not just skin cancer that could benefit from mRNA technology.
"Having succeeded in melanoma, this proof of concept could mark the beginning of a foundational shift in how we treat cancer, helping patients remain cancer-free for longer," says Long.
Alex Menzies, a medical oncologist at MIA, agrees.

"The hope for the near future is that it may not only improve outcomes for melanoma patients with advanced disease, but also those with other types of cancer where current immunotherapies are poorly effective," Menzies explains.
That's an exciting idea, but there is still more work to be done.
Recently, several randomized trials testing mRNA vaccines for colorectal cancer and for head and neck cancer have failed to reduce recurrence.
That makes these newest results even more important.

"The INTerpath-001 trial shows that treatment built from the unique signature of a patient's own tumor, working alongside checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy, can sharpen the immune system to find and destroy any remaining cancer cells," says Long.
"Just as email transformed how we communicate, individualized neoantigen therapy has the potential to transform how we treat cancer."
Charred coffee grounds could make concrete up to 30 percent stronger, scientists in Australia have found.
Their clever recipe could solve multiple problems at once.
Each year, the world produces about 10 billion kilograms (22 billion pounds) of coffee waste, most of which ends up in landfills.

"The disposal of organic waste poses an environmental challenge as it emits large amounts of greenhouse gases, including methane and carbon dioxide, which contribute to climate change," explained RMIT University engineer Rajeev Roychand when the research was first published in 2023.
With a booming construction market globally, there's an ever-increasing demand for resource-intensive concrete, causing another set of environmental challenges.
Watch the video below for a summary of the study:

"The ongoing extraction of natural sand around the world – typically taken from river beds and banks – to meet the rapidly growing demands of the construction industry has a big impact on the environment," said RMIT engineer Jie Li.

"There are critical and long-lasting challenges in maintaining a sustainable supply of sand due to the finite nature of resources and the environmental impacts of sand mining. With a circular-economy approach, we could keep organic waste out of landfill and also better preserve our natural resources like sand."
Organic products like coffee grounds can't be added directly to concrete because they leak chemicals that weaken the building material's strength.
So using low energy levels, the team heated coffee waste to over 350 °C (around 660 °F) while depriving it of oxygen.

This process is called pyrolysis. It breaks down the organic molecules, resulting in a porous, carbon-rich charcoal called biochar that can form bonds with and thereby incorporate itself into the cement matrix.
Roychand and colleagues also tried pyrolyzing the coffee grounds at 500 °C, but the resulting biochar particles were not as strong.
The researchers cautioned that they still need to assess the long-term durability of their cement product.
They're now working on testing how the hybrid coffee-cement performs under freeze/thaw cycles, water absorption, abrasions, and many more stressors.
The team is also working on creating biochars from other organic waste sources, including wood, food, and agricultural.

"Our research is in the early stages, but these exciting findings offer an innovative way to greatly reduce the amount of organic waste that goes to landfill," said RMIT engineer Shannon Kilmartin-Lynch.

"Inspiration for my research, from an Indigenous perspective, involves Caring for Country, ensuring there's a sustainable life cycle for all materials and avoiding things going into landfill to minimize the impact on the environment."
Related: One Way of Drinking Coffee Could Help You Live Longer, Study Finds

In 2024, RMIT and Macedon Ranges Shire Council poured a world-first real-world trial: a footpath in Gisborne, Victoria, made with the coffee biochar concrete alongside a wood-chip-biochar section and a standard-concrete control section.

Later that year, Victoria's Big Build used coffee-biochar concrete for a footpath on the Pakenham Roads Upgrade – the first major infrastructure project to use it – with contractor BildGroup estimating the job diverted roughly 140,000 coffees' worth of grounds from landfill and saved more than 3 metric tons (3.3 US tons) of sand.

In early 2025, the RMIT team picked up the People's Choice Problem Solver Award at Universities Australia's Shaping Australia Awards, and said they were working with a commercialization partner to build a business case to bring the material to market.
Their research was published in the Journal of Cleaner Production.

The world's pension systems are confronting a demographic crisis as longer lifespans and dwindling birth rates threaten to stretch retirement finances, raising questions about their ability to sustain payouts for future generations.

Pension offerings generally fall into two categories: defined-benefit plans, which promise retirees a predetermined income, and defined-contribution plans, where payouts depend on accumulated savings and investment returns.

Ageing poses different challenges for the two systems: defined-benefit schemes face mounting liabilities as retirees live longer, while defined-contribution members risk outliving their savings, placing greater pressure on funds' investment performance.

The problem is "huge, and it's gotten more pronounced over time,” said Sebastien Betermier, executive director at the International Centre for Pension Management, noting that some pension funds have members who have been retired for nearly half a century, aged aged 107 or 108.

"The higher the longevity, the more years the pension funds have to cover, and so that immediately comes in as an additional liability," he said. "Think about the cost that it imposes actually on the next generation … it is a ticking time bomb," Betermier told CNBC.

The scale of the challenge is laid bare in the 2026 Marsh CFA Institute Global Pension Index, or MCGPI, report published Tuesday last week. Of the 55 pension systems covered by the index, 43 have fertility rates below the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman, while 23 have rates below 1.5.

Meanwhile, life expectancy at age 65 in more developed regions has increased by 50.9% since 1950 to about 20 additional years, meaning retirement benefits must now last considerably longer. The number of potential workers supporting older people is also set to decline sharply.

“The funding of future pensions and aged care both become more critical as the ratio of workers to retirees continues to decline,” the MCGPI report stated. “Very few systems, as they currently operate, are secure.”

The problem is particularly acute for pay-as-you-go pension systems in which contributions from today's workers largely fund benefits for current retirees, leaving them especially vulnerable to a shrinking workforce.

The pressures are already evident in the U.S., where the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, which finances retirement and survivor benefits for tens of millions of Americans, is projected to exhaust its reserves in the fourth quarter of 2032, according to its latest trustees' report.
Fully funded pension schemes, which invest contributions from workers and employers to finance future retirement benefits are not immune either.

As their members retire and begin drawing down benefits, some funds could find themselves paying out more than they receive in fresh contributions, forcing them to rethink their investment strategies and liquidity needs, MCGPI cautioned.
“Future benefit outflows will exceed the level of contributions or premiums ... this financial strain will inevitably grow in the future,” the report highlighted.
The demographic crunch is reshaping how pension funds invest, with some taking on greater risks to generate the returns needed to meet growing retirement obligations.
Many mature funds are already paying out more in benefits than they receive in contributions, forcing them to rely increasingly on investment returns and accumulated assets.

In Australia, about a third of superannuation funds recorded negative natural cash flows from assets over a three-year period, meaning benefit payments exceeded contributions, according to a 2025 report by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority.
Industry watchers say the pressure to generate higher returns has pushed some funds toward riskier and more complex investments, including private equity, infrastructure and private credit.
"You can try to earn higher returns on your investments, but that's going to require taking on greater levels of risk," said Betermier.

Jean-Pierre Aubry, associate director of state and local research at the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College, said pension funds were increasingly shifting toward riskier investments, although the extent varied considerably across markets.
"I think everybody is shifting a little more risk where they can. The costs are going up with this demographic shift," Aubry said.
He pointed to U.S. state and local government pension funds, which hold only about 20% of their assets in bonds, with much of the remainder invested in equities and private assets.
Such allocations make U.S. public pension funds considerably more exposed to investment risk than their counterparts in Europe and Canada, he said.
Not every pension manager sees ageing as a reason to take bigger bets.
David Elias, CEO of Australian pension fund Hostplus said demographic changes were only one of many factors shaping investment decisions.
He stressed the importance of maintaining a diversified portfolio across asset classes, geographies and industries, while ensuring that potential returns adequately compensate for the risks involved.

Elias also said that governments could find ways to mitigate the pressures of ageing populations, including through immigration policies and technological advances, while demographic shifts themselves could create new investment opportunities.
"I don't underestimate governments being incredibly creative in terms of dealing with these types of issues," he said. "You know, but they're going to have to address it, no doubt about that."
U.S. crude oil fell over 2% on Monday as investors weighed the threat of further attacks on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure against concerns that elevated prices could eventually erode demand.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures slid 2.19% to $101 a barrel, while Brent crude futures declined 1.89% to $114.51 a barrel.
The pullback followed a sharp rally on Friday after attacks by Yemen's Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia reignited fears of disruptions to global energy supplies.

Tensions remained elevated over the weekend as the Houthis said they had targeted Saudi Arabia's main airport in Riyadh and oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities said Sunday that they had intercepted additional missiles and drones.
The kingdom partially resumed operations at its main airport on Sunday despite damage from earlier attacks, even as the Houthis threatened further strikes.

The continued hostilities have heightened concerns about the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure, with traders increasingly focused on the risk of a major disruption to production, refining or export facilities.
Speaking to CNBC, Michael Alfaro, chief investment officer at Gallo Partners, estimated that geopolitical uncertainty had already added roughly $20 a barrel to oil prices.
A substantial strike on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline or additional refining infrastructure could send prices sharply higher, he added, but further gains could eventually undermine consumption.
"What we would likely see if oil pushed above 120, 130, 140 dollars a barrel for Brent, that is, you're going to see more demand destruction," Alfaro said.
Beyond the immediate threat to crude supplies, damage to refining infrastructure could pose a more persistent challenge to global energy markets.
"The real challenge is refining capacity," he said, warning that the disruptions could develop into a longer-term structural problem extending into 2027 and beyond.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia plans to begin storing crude oil in Singapore from the second half of 2027, according to energy ministers from both countries, in a move aimed at strengthening the resilience of its Asian supply chain.
In the U.S., the Energy Department on Friday authorized the release of up to 400,000 barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address a supply disruption at a Louisiana refinery.
Still, the prospect of additional supply from American producers remains uncertain, with companies reluctant to commit to major new investments amid volatile prices and geopolitical risks.
Alfaro added that U.S. producers were adding some drilling rigs, but remained cautious about substantially increasing capital expenditure.
"We're not really seeing major capex additions to bring new rigs on or bring new production online," he said.
