Jack White is mourning the death of his older brother, Edward “Eddie” Gillis, who managed Third Man Records’ Detroit vinyl pressing plant.

White shared the news in an Instagram post on Saturday (Oct. 24), writing that Gillis had died that morning “after having fought a tough battle against cancer.” “The world lost a beautiful soul today,” White wrote. “Ed was such a caring, funny and generous person that everybody loved.”

Gillis ran Third Man Pressing for 10 years, overseeing the production of “hundreds of thousands” of records for other artists, White wrote, adding that his brother liked to make small sculptures and flowers from the plant’s vinyl scraps. The facility opened in 2017 in Detroit’s Cass Corridor as part of White’s Third Man Records operation, making White one of the few artists to own his own pressing plant. Before that, Gillis worked as a pastry chef, running kitchens and bake shops for the Ritz-Carlton and Beaumont Hospital.

White, the youngest of 10 siblings, also credited Gillis with shaping his musical start. “In his youth Eddie was the guitar player in the family when we were all growing up back when I was on drums only, and he was just great at the instrument,” he wrote, recalling that the two played together over the years, once for the Detroit Tigers during spring training in Florida. “He taught me so many wonderful and simple things over the years that I’ll never forget; how to string a guitar, how to fish on the Detroit river, how to drive a stick shift,” White added. “He was an amazing big brother to me and I just hate to see him leave, but I’m glad he is at peace.”
Gillis is survived by his wife, Angie, and their two children, Amelia and Garrett.

White rose to fame as one half of the White Stripes, whose “Seven Nation Army” topped Billboard’s Alternative Airplay chart. As a solo artist, he has sent three albums to No. 1 on the Billboard 200: Blunderbuss (2012), Lazaretto (2014) and Boarding House Reach (2018). Lazaretto also set the record for the biggest vinyl sales week since 1991, a mark it held until 2021.

Lady Lava may have dominated the night with four wins, including female soca artist of the year and zess song of the year (“Bob the Builder”), but the fourth annual Caribbean Music Awards certainly avoided clean sweeps.

Co-hosted by Majah Hype and soca star Nailah Blackman at Trinidad & Tobago’s National Academy for the Performing Arts (NAPA) in Port of Spain on Sept. 18, this year’s Caribbean Music Awards marked the first time the ceremony took place in its namesake region. The official broadcast premiered on the official Caribbean Music Awards YouTube page on Oct. 25, delivering a star-studded celebration of the biggest and brightest stars across the contemporary Caribbean music scene.

This year, several new categories were added to the ceremony’s sprawling lineup, including much-needed spotlights of fast-rising genres like bouyon, jab and Dennery segment. Billboard’s Kyle Denis hosted a red carpet livestream on the ground in Trinidad, catching up with a bevy of stars, including eventual winners Kes and Ayetian, as well as the night’s biggest victor, Lady Lava.

Outside of Lava, several other acts took home multiple trophies at this year’s ceremony. Trinidadian brother production duo Full Blown took home three awards, including soca song of the year for “The Greatest Bend Over” (with Yung Bredda) and soca video of the year for “Good Spirits.” They tied as this year’s second-most awarded act alongside pop-dancehall princess Shenseea and French-Haitian konpa singer Joé Dwèt Filé, who swept the konpa and French-Caribbean fields with his smash hit “4 Kampé.” Skillibeng, Kes, V’ghn, Lila Iké, Masicka, Moliy, Ayetian, Silent Addy, and Ravi B also snagged multiple awards.

In addition to over 50 competitive awards, several Caribbean music legends were honored for their timeless contributions to the culture. Billboard Hot 100-charting reggae and dancehall queen Patra earned the Lifetime Achievement Award; Victoire de la Musique winner Calypso Rose received the Elite Calypso Award; konpa giant Alan Cavé scored the Elite Konpa Award; and Belizean-born, Brooklyn-bred hip-hop and political icon Shyne snagged the Global Ambassador Award.
While the ceremony certainly had its heartwarming moments, there were also quite a few head-scratchers. Here are six of the biggest snubs and surprises from the fan-voted 2026 Caribbean Music Awards.

- Surprise: ‘Dansa’ Wins Dennery Segment Song of the Year When Klassik Frescobar’s “Dansa” was announced as the winner of Dennery segment song of the year, Saint Lucian Twitter was almost instantly set ablaze. Dennery segment, an offshoot of soca combining elements of kuduro and zouk with Kwéyòl lyrics and dancehall-esque attitude, was developed in Saint Lucia’s Dennery District. It’s a fast-rising, distinctly Lucian sound that finally got a spotlight at the Caribbean Music Awards for the first time this year, so it was no surprise that a Jamaican-American (Frescobar) beating out an all-Lucian lineup of songs would ruffle some feathers. The other nominees in the category were: “Clap” (Blackboy), “Freak Out” (Hollywood HP & Ricky T), “Life of Party” (Pimp Juice), “Nuh Nuh” (Mighty & Mikado), “Pain Killer” (Umpa & Mikado), “The Car” (Dezral & Jardel) and “Toko Doak” (Natoxie & Deejay Asap). While Frescobar recorded “Dansa” over a beat helmed by Lucian Dennery segment producer DJ Kalli, the track is closer to late-2010s Dennery segment than the genre’s current sound — and it’s notably lacking the Kwéyòl lyrics that are a foundational element of the style. In a TikTok posted to his official account a week after the ceremony, Frescobar joked that he was “just as confused as you guys were,” and Umpa, who won Dennery segment artist of the year, recently told Billboard that “‘Dansa’ had the potential to win’ because of its crossover commercial success relative to the rest of the nominees. Ultimately, this should’ve gone to a Lucian Dennery segment artist — preferably “Nuh Nuh” by Mighty and Mikado.

- Snub: Lil Kerry & Muddy Go Home Empty-Handed Lil Kerry and Muddy have been instrumental in raising the Grenadian soca scene’s profile over the past year. Kerry clinched this year’s Grenada Road March title with his pulsating “Mayhem,” while Muddy landed a spot on Rolling Stone’s Best Songs of 2025 with his equally electric “Payroll.” Both artists also brought their high-octane, road-ready energy to the Caribbean Music Awards stage in NAPA, and they both earned nominations in this year’s newly established categories of jab artist of the year and jab song of the year. Nonetheless, neither artist could take down V’ghn, whose Terra D Governor-assisted “Jab Decisions” — a notable departure from his usual groovy soca — swept the jab field. Surely, we could’ve spread the wealth for a genre with just two categories?

- Surprise: Prince Swanny Wins Dancehall Album of the Year Dancehall is one of Jamaica’s biggest cultural exports, so it’s always a surprise when an artist from another island snags an award in the genre. Trinidad’s very own Prince Swanny won dancehall album of the year for his slinky, sultry Saint LP, beating out a stacked up line-up that included Masicka (Her Name Is Love), Popcaan (Nothing Without Love), 450 (Pieces of Me), Valiant (Prove Them Wrong), Armanii (The Impact), Vybz Kartel (Viking – 10th Anniversary Edition) and Ding Dong (From Ding Dong to World Ding).

- Snub: Machel Montano & Ayetian Come Up Short in Soca Collaboration of the Year King of Soca Machel Montano and Ayetian, Billboard’s Caribbean Up-And-Comer of the Month for July 2026, scored one of the most beloved and infectious crossover soca hits of recent years with “Truth & Balance,” but even they proved no match for the power of Nicki Minaj’s Barbz. The Trinidad-born, Queens-bred rapper coasted to a victory in soca collaboration of the year, thanks to her dedicated fan base rallying around her “Eskimo” link-up with zess artist Trinidad Killa.

- Surprise: Masicka Snags Dancehall Video of the Year Last year, Shenseea, Masicka, and Di Genius cleaned up in the dancehall category with “Hit & Run,” winning song, video, and collaboration of the year. This year, Moliy attempted to do the same with “Shake It to the Max” — which also features Shenseea, alongside Skillibeng, Silent Addy and Disco Neil — but Masicka thwarted her attempt at a clean sweep by taking home dancehall video of the year for his steamy “Rich Sex” visual.

- Snub: Bunji Garlin Shut Out for Second Consecutive Year Justice for Bunji Garlin! Last year, the soca powerhouse came up short for all three of his nominations — and history repeated this year. Garlin earned nods for male soca artist of the year, soca song of the year (“Carry It”), and soca collaboration of the year (“Flatten,” with Voice). Admittedly, the soca field was especially competitive this year, but “Carry It” truly deserved recognition for its expert balance of deft, culture-rooted lyricism and downright galvanizing melody.

From the continued domination of Full Blown’s “Big Links” riddim and Kes’ globe-trotting touring success to major moments like Destin Conrad’s Roadrunner reggae-dancehall LP and Keznamdi’s triumphant Grammy win, it’s been quite the year for Caribbean music and culture. Several Caribbean music giants were honored for their impact and influence. Billboard Hot 100-charting reggae and dancehall powerhouse Patra scored the Lifetime Achievement Award; global music icon Calypso Rose received the Elite Calypso Award; Cavé earned the Elite Konpa Award; and hip-hop giant Shyne took home the Global Ambassador Award.
Here are the six best moments from the 2026 Caribbean Music Awards.

- Yung Bredda Brings ‘Greatest Bend Over’ Full Circle Yung Bredda’s “Greatest Bend Over” was easily the biggest song on Full Blown’s incredibly successful “Big Links” riddim last year, so it was a shame that he was unable to join the brother duo (and Machel Montano and Ayetian) for their crowd-rocking “Big Links” medley at last year’s ceremony. When Majah Hype announced “Greatest Bend Over” as this year’s winner of soca song of the year, Bredda accepted the award in person alongside Full Blown — and in his home country, for that matter. Not only is the song still fresh, but this full-circle moment also made the whole riddim even sweeter. “First things first, I want to say ‘Thank you’ to the Most High God; you know I always put God first in everything,” he began his acceptance speech. “Thank you for such a wonderful team that I have behind me… we coming from since COVID time ’til now, and [we have] an even further journey to go. I want to thank each and every person out there that’s been supporting what we’re doing and all my music.”

- MOLIY Hits Her Signature ‘Shake It to the Max’ Dance While Accepting Award “Shake It to the Max” may have ultimately been deemed ineligible to compete for the 2026 Grammys, but MOLIY still got her awards moment for her career-skyrocketing dancehall crossover smash. Alongside collaborators Shenseea, Skillibeng, Silent Addy and Disco Neil, MOLIY beat out an incredibly stacked lineup that included Skippa (“WYFL”), Armanii (“BBB – Snapchat”), Jada Kingdom (“G.A.D.”), Vybz Kartel (“God Is the Greatest”), Valiant (“Passenger Princess”), Masicka (“Rich Sex”) and Ayetian & Govana (“Wah Yo Deh Pan”). MOLIY also won dancehall collaboration of the year for “Shake It to the Max.” Once Yung Bredda announced “Shake It to the Max” as the winner, MOLIY hit her signature waist-whining, hands-covering-face dance move before making her way to the stage. “When I wrote this song, I had no idea the doors it would open for me,” she said, her face beaming with pride and excitement. “I had no idea I would be welcomed into this amazing community. - Alison Hinds Pops Out to Honor Patra Last year, Bajan soca superstar Alison Hinds made an appearance and gave a sweet shoutout to fellow Bajan musician Rihanna to celebrate 20 years of her classic debut single, “Pon De Replay.” This year, Hinds honored another fellow powerhouse woman when she presented Patra with the Lifetime Achievement Award. Patra, a Jamaican reggae star who frequently charted on the Billboard Hot 100 in the mid-’90s and recently starred in the buzzy British television series Get Millie Back, joins previous Lifetime Achievement honorees, including Marcia Griffiths, Machel Montano and Bounty Killer. Fittingly, Patra also closed out the ceremony with a career-spanning medley of hits. “I’ve gone through a lot, but I’m happy now,” Patra said during her tearful acceptance speech. “And, to my fans, you guys have been holding me down for years… I highly recommend to you ladies: Please love yourselves. And take care of yourself. Don’t be afraid to be alone and reassess stuff. Love who you are, okay? And stop going around talking about aging and being ungrateful. Be thankful!”

- Jah Mason Celebrates Legacy of ‘My Princess Gone’ Jah Mason’s “My Princess Gone” is arguably one of the most beloved reggae ballads of the 21st century, and Mason proved as much when he took the stage to perform the classic at the 2026 Caribbean Music Awards. Taking the stage shortly after 450’s dancehall-driven set, Mason immediately spiked the crowd’s energy with the opening notes of “Princess,” and by the time the first chorus hit, the audience practically sang the song for him. Inside the NAPA, it was particularly difficult to loosen up the Caribbean Music Awards crowd, but Mason did so with little effort at all.

- Grenada Takes Center Stage with V’ghn, Lil Kerry & Muddy From Spicemas to jab jab, Grenada has significantly upped its profile on the international stage this year. At the 2026 Caribbean Music Awards, three of the island nation’s most resonant voices — V’ghn, Lil Kerry and Muddy — mounted a high-energy medley of their three jab-hailing soca hits. In 2019, Rose made her Coachella debut at 78 years old, marking the first time a calypso artist played a full set at the iconic festival and cementing her as the two-weekend extravaganza’s oldest performer to date. After a video package ran through Rose’s decades-long career, Lyons led the packed audience in a singalong of “Calypso Queen,” featuring animated ad-libs from the Queen of Calypso herself. Oct. 26 (UPI) -- Serbia's longtime nationalist leader Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat Sunday in snap parliamentary elections to a student-led opposition movement.
"It is clear that we have lost these elections," Vucic told supporters at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party as the results came in, according to a statement from his party.

"We don't have the final results. Many will be surprised, and you will realize how much some people have lied and what they have fabricated. I want to inform you that the student-led protest list has won."
The defeat of Vucic, who resigned as president Sept. 27 to seek a return to the prime minister's office, which he held from 2014 to 2017, followed two years of student-led protests.

According to projections by the independent election-monitoring organization Center for Free Elections and Democracy, the Student List was expected to win 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament and Vucic's SNS won 103 seats, with a handful of minority parties winning the remaining seven seats, Serbian news agency FoNet reported.
Radomir Saicic, an academic and a Student List candidate, celebrated the results Sunday night at the movement's headquarters in New Belgrade.
"This is a victory of courage over fear, a victory of hope over indifference, a victory of faith that Serbia can and must be different," he said, Beta news agency reported.

"Thank you for every step, every hour, every sacrifice and every moment in which you chose not to give up. Thank you to everyone who raised their voice, who stood together and who showed that the future of this country does not belong to a select few, but to all its citizens."

The snap election was called on Sept. 9, when Vucic dissolved parliament amid nearly two years of anti-government protests by students initially angry over the deaths of 16 people in the Nov. 1, 2024, collapse of a concrete canopy at Novi Sad railway station, viewing the incident as the product of government corruption and negligence.
The election results could have significant implications for the Balkan nation.

Under Vucic's rule, the country maintained close relations with Russia. Russian President Vladimir Putin had publicly expressed support for Vucic's run for the premiership. While the Student List campaigned on Serbia maintaining its stance against imposing sanctions against Russia, it also expressed support Ukraine's territorial integrity.

The victory could also signal closer ties with the European Union, although the Student List has pledged to maintain Serbia's traditional relations with Russia. Serbia has been a candidate for EU membership since 2012, but negotiations have largely stalled since 2021 under Vucic's leadership.

"Today, the people of Serbia turned out in record numbers to shape their country's future. Congratulations to the Student List on its victory in the parliamentary elections," EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.

"We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia's future in the European Union."
Marta Kos, EU commissioner for enlargement, said the election means "a new chapter can begin for Serbia."

"After nearly two years of protests for democracy, the rule of law and the fight against corruption, Serbians turned out in historic numbers," she said online, saying, "These are the very values at the heart of the European Union."
"The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together."

Oct. 25 (UPI) -- A federal appeals court panel, meeting in a rare Sunday session, appeared skeptical of arguments by the Trump administration as it pressed its demand for the state of California to set aside 20,000 ballots it claims could be cast by non-citizens.

The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, based in San Francisco, convened on a videoconference two days after the Trump administration urged it to intervene in their lawsuit demanding that California election officials access a password-protected flash drive they say has the names of thousands of possible non-citizens believed to be on the state's voter registration list.
U.S. District Judge David Carter had already scheduled an emergency hearing on the matter for Tuesday but the Department of Justice sought and received an appellate court intervention on Sunday.

U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter last week gave the Los Angeles County Clerk and California Secretary of State two days to confirm they were reviewing the thousands of submitted names and were segregating possible ballots, which may have been cast by individuals listed on the thumb drive.

California officials called the request legally baseless and a last-ditch effort by the White House to intervene in next week's midterm elections, even after losing more than two dozen court challenges over the past year to force states to release their voter rolls.
During Sunday's hearing, the appellate judges appeared similarly skeptical, peppering the DOJ lawyers with pointed questions.

After government attorney Matthew Donnelly said the Trump administration came up with the names after carrying out a "rigorous process" using its own citizenship data, Judge Mark Bennett questioned whether state election workers could legally disqualify voters without "extraordinary proof" by the federal government.

"Congress and the California Legislature have said non-citizens can't vote. This lawsuit is about, 'We don't like the way you're sorting citizens from non-citizens,'" Bennett stated. "I just don't see [federal law] telling California how to do the sorting."

Judge Gabriel Sanchez, an appointee of President Joe Biden, also expressed significant skepticism about the legality of the remedies being sought by the Trump administration so close to election day and whether appellate court intervention is appropriate at this point.
California's attorney Samuel Siegel said the White House lacks the constitutional authority to tell California how to sort its ballots.

"If the federal government, if the Executive Branch wants that authority in the first instance, they need to go ask Congress for it, they haven't done that," Siegel said. "They ask this court to short circuit the democratic process and issue an order, not just on the eve of an election, but as an election is underway."
Oct. 25 (UPI) -- A 20-year-old U.S. Marine has been charged in the killing and robbing of a Japanese woman at a hotel in Okinawa.

Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard was indicted Sunday on a charge of robbery causing death in the killing of 39-year-old Anna Yagi, according to a copy of the indictment provided by the Naha Public Prosectors Office.

Prosecutors allege Ballard wrapped a telephone handset cord around Yagi's neck early on Oct. 3 "with intent to kill." They said he killed her and stole her backpack, which contained a wallet and other items.
Ballard, who has denied the allegations, was arrested the next day, the Okinawa Prefectural Police said.
He faces the death penalty or life in prison, if convicted.
III Marine Expeditionary Force is continuing to cooperate with the investigation, spokesman 1st Lt. Tyle Thomas said.
"We recognize the seriousness of the charges and will continue to cooperate fully with Japanese authorities in their ongoing investigation as the legal process moves forward," he said.

The arrest of Billard has increased scrutiny of the conduct of U.S. military personnel on Okinawa. Gov. Gent Koja and the prefecture's assembly have demanded a review of the pact that governs U.S. military-connected personnel in Japan.
III MEF commander Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson imposed a 30-day midnight-to-5 a.m. curfew for U.S. troops on Okinawa through Nov. 8.

Across hundreds of miles of the northern Gulf of Mexico, a deepwater ecosystem collapsed after the massive 2011 Deepwater Horizon oil and gas spill, and recovery is uncertain, new research concludes.

The study, published Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, found that animal populations—including octopus, krill, squid, and shrimp—declined by 60 to 85 percent in the three and a half years after the spill, with few signs of recovery since. Krill and lanternfish, both foundational species in the Gulf’s food web, were among the hardest hit. The findings also suggest that the die-off is causing genetic bottlenecks that could further hinder ecosystem recovery.

The researchers identified it as the “fastest and most severe faunal decline reported for Earth’s largest ecosystem type” ever documented. The widespread die-off of marine organisms may also reduce the ocean’s ability to transport carbon dioxide from the atmosphere to the deep sea. After ruling out other factors, such as water temperature and oxygen levels, the researchers identified the Deepwater Horizon blowout as “the most parsimonious explanation” for the ecosystem’s collapse.

Comprehensive natural resource damage assessments and restoration efforts involving federal, state, and tribal trustees are ongoing. In 2016, BP agreed to a $20.8 billion settlement, including up to $8.8 billion for environmental restoration.

Remote ocean depths and habitats miles below the surface may seem buffered from the impacts of human activity, the authors wrote, but their findings suggest an industrial disaster pushed part of it into a diminished state with “limited resilience to facilitate recovery.” They said their findings also show that proposed industrial deep-sea mining could damage the ecosystem before baseline conditions are assessed.

A transoceanic drilling rig, operating for BP about 50 miles southeast of the Mississippi Delta, exploded on April 20, 2010. The explosion and fire killed 11 people and triggered the largest accidental marine oil spill in history.

Oil and gas spewed uncontrollably from the broken well nearly a mile deep for 87 days, ejecting 4.9 million barrels of oil at a rate of about 400 tanker trucks per day, enough to fill up 1.2 million cars. The spill also released about 7.7 billion cubic feet of fossil gas into the deep sea at a rate of 88 million cubic feet per day, enough to supply about 820,000 US homes. State and federal agencies, including the Environmental Protection Agency, also authorized BP to apply 1.84 million gallons of chemical dispersants to try to reduce the impacts.

Some of the oil and gas dissipated and was transported out of the deep Gulf of Mexico region. Some coated barrier islands and devastated coastal wetlands and shellfish habitat, and some settled onto the ocean floor, where currents can stir it back into the water. But enough hydrocarbon and chemical-dispersant remnants stayed suspended long enough to do almost immeasurable harm.

A series of studies since the spill have shown a wide range of toxic effects on marine organisms, from impaired development and reproduction to increased mortality and lasting health problems in dolphins and whales. The new paper suggests that lingering pollutants may interfere with some species’ ability to find mates in the dark by disrupting their highly developed sense of smell.

The impacts continue to ripple through the ecosystem, said lead author Tracey Sutton, a professor of marine and environmental sciences at Nova Southeastern University in Florida. A 2024 study found an 80 percent decline in deep-diving toothed whales, he said.

“We used to have a big resident population of sperm whales right off the Mississippi River, but we haven’t seen a sperm whale in 10 years,” he said. Large predators need big, occasional dense patches of prey, and those have disappeared, he added.

Scientists have developed accurate ways to count fish. For this study, they started with a baseline from nine months of sampling in 2011 and compared it with nine subsequent surveys between 2015 and 2023. The researchers sampled deep-pelagic habitat along a large grid around the spill site from about 650 feet below the surface to about a mile down. The deep-pelagic zone accounts for about 90 percent of the Gulf’s total volume.

Across a grid of stations, scientists on slippery decks lowered and hoisted nets that open and close at different depths, with experts from different species groups to identify the catch. They sampled around noon and midnight to account for species that migrate vertically each day. Ship-mounted scientific echosounders provided an independent check, measuring sound reflected by marine life in the water column.

The research is “comprehensive and carefully composed,” marine biologist Bruce Robison, a senior scientist at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, said via email. “There is no other study that I know of with such an incredible number of net samples,” added Robison, who did not participate in the new study.
The research focuses on species that are not commercially fished and shows for the first time that human impacts can deplete marine life even in very deep ocean water, he said.

“It is important for the public to understand just how disastrous this oil spill was,” Robison said. “The Gulf has not recovered, and it’s been over 15 years.” Robison said other activities, such as deep-sea mining, could also have severe negative consequences for deepwater pelagic ecosystems by discharging wastewater containing metals or lubricants.

Three lines of evidence—net hauls, acoustic surveys, and genetic sampling—corroborate each other, which is “unusually strong evidence to support his conclusions,” said Jeffrey Drazen, a marine ecologist at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, who did not participate in the new study.
The study examines all possible causes of the decline and shows only one aligns with the scientific evidence, he said.
“Through logical elimination,” he said, “and without actually pointing a finger, they leave no doubt that the oil spill is the cause of the decline.”
Android Auto and CarPlay have transformed the way people drive.

Rather than putting up with whatever infotainment systems car manufacturers have put together, we're now able to interact with our phones from our car dashboards—with our contacts, our music, our podcasts, and our mapping apps all available. And the list of supported vehicles just keeps growing.

Both the Google and Apple solutions for this are really simple to use too. Most of the time they'll connect up automatically once you've done the initial setup. What you might not realize, though, are the demands that Android Auto and CarPlay put on your phone. Your handset is essentially doing all the regular phone stuff and then powering a large tablet-like display at the same time. That typically includes constantly updating a map in real time.

With that in mind, your Android phone or iPhone can quickly start to lose battery life and heat up when it's connected to your vehicle, which you've perhaps already noticed. To keep your handset cool and your battery in good shape, here's what you need to do.
Go Wired if You Can (but Watch the Charging)

Wireless Android Auto and CarPlay are convenient, just like wireless charging is convenient, but it puts more stress on your phone. If you've got the option of a wired connection, that's preferable—but that introduces a new potential heat problem, which is that your phone will always be charging up.
To counter that, you can set charge limits (Battery and charging from Android Settings, Battery > Charging from iOS Settings), or simply make sure your phone is kept in a cool, dark spot of the car.

This wired option has the added bonus of letting you switch to airplane mode on your phone, which will go a long way to limiting heat. Again there's a trade-off though: No one will be able to reach you, and you'll need to have your maps, music, podcasts, and whatever else you need downloaded to your device in advance.

If you do stick with wireless Android Auto or CarPlay, try to avoid charging your phone at the same time, especially on the wireless pad built into the car’s dash (which generates more heat). You don't want to end up with a dead phone half way through the journey, so you may have to compromise at certain times.

As mentioned above, where your phone is in the car makes a real difference to how hot it's going to be. If you have your phone's interface up on your car dashboard, then you don't necessarily need to have it fixed to the dashboard, too, possibly under direct sunlight. The glove compartment will do just fine.

If you have a mount for your phone, think about attaching it in front of one of your car's air vents. Blasts of air conditioned air will significantly reduce how hot your handset gets, working like a DIY cooling system.

You might also want to think about taking the case off of your phone for the length of the trip, if your phone is fitted with one. Your handset is less likely to be dropped or knocked while you're driving anyway, and a case can trap the heat in.

The rules aren't too different to keeping your phone cool generally, though with the added wrinkle of needing to keep it connected to your car somehow. Make sure the cabin in general is at a comfortable temperature, though you're probably already doing that for your own sake. The bigger thing to remember is to avoid leaving your phone behind in a vehicle that's going to heat up in the sun if you're stopping off somewhere.

If your phone is hooked up to Android Auto or CarPlay, then it's probably got some work to do—whether it's getting you to a destination or streaming music. However, you can still reduce heat by keeping phone tasks down to a minimum. If your calls and (voice-activated) messages can wait, leave them until the end of the journey.

We mentioned offline syncing above, but it doesn't have to go along with airplane mode. If you sync your tunes, podcasts, and maps to your phone ahead of time, your handset has less work to do while you’re driving since it doesn’t need to pull data from the cloud while also constantly searching for a wireless signal as you travel. Less stress on the modem means less heat overall.

Both Apple Maps and Google Maps let you download maps ahead of a trip. In Apple Maps, tap your profile picture, then Offline Maps, then Add Offline Map and find your location. With Google Maps, tap your profile picture, then choose Offline maps > Select your own map to choose the coverage.

There may be times when your phone has to be charging, wirelessly connected, making calls, in direct sunlight, and streaming music over a cellular connection, but try to keep these times to a minimum. Check regularly on how hot your phone is getting while connected to Android Auto or CarPlay, so you can take action if needed.

According to a new report from MarketsandMarkets, the vehicle electrification market will grow from $54.9 billion in 2026 to $87.8 billion by 2033. The market will expand at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6.9% during the forecast period. Regulatory frameworks, including strict carbon dioxide emissions standards, zero-emission mandates and fleet decarbonization targets, have become primary demand drivers. These requirements have shifted beyond compliance costs, making policy timelines leading indicators for new automotive platform launches.

Meanwhile, high-utilization commercial fleets are reaching total cost of ownership (TCO) parity first. This trend makes electrification an investment decision driven by return on investment (ROI). Rapid paybacks on electrified auxiliaries, start-stop systems and integrated starter generators support these investments.

Additionally, the transition toward 800-volt architectures and battery-electric vehicle (BEV) platforms increases component value per vehicle. These platforms incorporate higher-margin components, including electric power steering, positive temperature coefficient (PTC) heaters and electric compressors. This allows suppliers to increase revenue per vehicle faster than overall vehicle production volumes.
Infrastructure Challenges Affect Vehicle Electrification Market Growth
However, energy infrastructure availability and economics now represent the industry’s primary growth constraints, rather than vehicle technology or baseline demand.

Grid capacity limitations, megawatt charging speeds and high deployment costs continue to restrict mass-market expansion. These challenges concentrate early adoption among commercial fleets and fixed-route applications.
This infrastructure gap creates an imbalance between demand and supply that component manufacturers must navigate.

Near-term revenue growth will remain concentrated in privately funded fleet operations. Meanwhile, broader market expansion depends on utility upgrades, public policy and capital investment cycles outside the automotive industry’s direct control.
Passenger Cars Expected to Hold Largest Market Share

The passenger car segment will likely account for the largest share of the vehicle electrification market. Passenger cars dominate because electrification extends beyond propulsion into steering, braking, thermal management, HVAC and power distribution.

Consequently, individual vehicles incorporate numerous electrified components, including electric power steering, electric compressors, electric pumps, PTC heaters and integrated starter generators. Advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), infotainment technology and increasingly complex thermal requirements further accelerate this trend.

As Bosch highlights, the convergence of electrification, automation, and connectivity is driving the transition to centralized zonal architectures and elevated powernet demands to support these next-generation x-by-wire capabilities.

Passenger cars offer opportunities to increase electrification content per vehicle, beyond their large share of vehicle production. Passenger car platforms include 12-volt, 48-volt mild-hybrid, hybrid-electric, plug-in hybrid and 400- to 800-volt BEV architectures. This diversity allows suppliers to offer multiple electrification technologies across a broad customer base.

For example, Valeo offers low- and high-voltage electrification, 48-volt hybrid systems, electric motors and thermal management technologies. Its portfolio supports various passenger car architectures. Meanwhile, Bosch integrates powertrain, thermal and battery management functions into its vehicle-control architecture.

These developments create multiple revenue opportunities as passenger cars transition toward electrically actuated, software-controlled platforms. Electrification continues expanding beyond powertrains into steering, thermal management, braking and auxiliary functions.
Liquid PTC Heaters Expected to Lead EV Product Growth

Liquid PTC heaters will likely become the fastest-growing electrification product in the electric vehicle (EV) segment during the forecast period. These heaters address a fundamental BEV design challenge: the absence of engine waste heat.

Unlike internal combustion engine vehicles, BEVs cannot rely on engine-heated coolant for cabin heating or battery conditioning. Instead, high-voltage liquid PTC heaters directly heat coolant circulating through battery, cabin heating and other thermal systems.

Their importance increases with larger batteries, fast charging, cold-weather operation and stricter battery temperature requirements. These heaters rapidly precondition batteries before charging or driving and maintain operating temperatures. They directly influence charging performance, power availability and battery durability.

For example, BorgWarner offers high-voltage coolant heaters operating between 250 and 800 volts, with outputs ranging from 3 to 10 kilowatts. The company has secured programs across BEV and plug-in hybrid platforms, including 400- and 800-volt applications.
Thermal Management Technologies Expand Applications

Liquid PTC heaters are evolving beyond cabin heating into essential components of vehicle thermal management systems. Modern systems increasingly combine these heaters with heat pumps, coolant pumps, valves and waste-heat recovery technologies.

These combinations direct heat toward functions that deliver the greatest vehicle-level benefits. Applications include battery preconditioning before fast charging, cabin heating with reduced range loss and battery temperature management under extreme conditions.

Webasto’s latest architecture integrates high-voltage heaters with coolant and refrigerant circuits. Its Heated Chiller combines previously separate functions, reducing component counts and system complexity.
The expansion of high-voltage coolant heater programs into 800-volt platforms and plug-in hybrids also broadens the technology’s potential market.

The Mustang Mach-E uses Ford’s Global Electrified 1 (GE1) platform, a heavily reworked version of the automaker’s C2 architecture. The C2 platform also underpins the fourth-generation Ford Focus and third-generation Kuga, as well as the fourth-generation Escape. While the Mach-E shares its platform lineage with these vehicles, GE1 was adapted for an all-electric SUV. That platform connection provides useful context for technicians approaching its suspension and alignment service, while vehicle-specific procedures and specifications remain essential across model years and configurations.

The Mustang Mach-E has adjustable camber and toe at both ends, but an alignment service with this car also calls for attention to the vehicle loading, ride height and driver-assistance systems. The procedures provided in this article are for a 2023 AWD Mach-E, so confirm the specifications and service procedure for the vehicle’s exact model year and configuration before making adjustments. The supplied information does not include numerical alignment specifications or acceptable ride-height ranges.

Before measuring toe, Ford’s procedure calls for a level surface, correct tire pressure, and an inspection for tire wear, damage and suspension wear or damage. The steering wheel must be held straight ahead with a suitable holding device during the toe checks.

Ride-height measurement has additional preparation requirements. Position the vehicle on a flat, level surface with tires inflated to the correct pressure. The procedure specifies a full tank of fuel, proper fluid levels and no cargo in the cabin or bed. Inspect for aftermarket equipment and changes to steering, suspension, wheels or tires, then jounce the front and rear suspension vigorously to let the vehicle settle.

Remember: Alignment readings are only useful when the vehicle is in the specified condition. If ride height is incorrect, look for changes or problems in the suspension and review the vehicle’s service information before treating alignment adjustments as the solution.

If you find that you can’t get the vehicle to roll to carry out the rolling compensation measurements, this is because it has Rollaway Protection Mode that activates when the car is turned off and the driver exits. To enable the car to roll, you will have to leave it on and in neutral during the alignment. In some cases, you might want to attach the driver seatbelt and roll the door latch to prevent it from going into park.

Front camber is adjusted at the strut-to-knuckle connection. First, measure camber with alignment equipment, then remove the wheels and tires. The brake flexible hose is unbolted and moved aside, and the wheel knuckle is supported with mechanic’s wire.

The original strut-to-knuckle bolts and nuts are removed and discarded. Ford specifies new service bolts and nuts for reassembly. The service fasteners are smooth and smaller in diameter than the splined original equipment bolts. With the new fasteners installed and snug, move the knuckle inboard or outboard to bring camber into specification. The procedure states that moving from the maximum inboard to maximum outboard position provides 0.5 degree of adjustment.

Do not fully tighten the strut-to-knuckle fasteners until camber is corrected. After adjustment, torque the bolts and nuts to 173 lb.-ft. (235 Nm). Reinstall the brake hose and torque its bolt to 97 lb.-in. (11 Nm). Reinstall the wheels and tires, recheck alignment and adjust front toe if needed. Because changing camber can affect toe, finish by verifying the toe readings.

Front toe is adjusted at the inner tie rods. With the steering wheel held straight, check toe on both sides. Hold each outer tie-rod end stationary while loosening its jam nut; Ford cautions that allowing the tie-rod end to turn can damage the boot. Move the steering gear boot clamp aside, then rotate the inner tie rod to adjust toe. Do not let the steering gear bellows twist as the inner tie rod turns. Recheck toe after adjustment and road test the vehicle.

Rear camber is adjusted by moving the upper control arm at its inboard mounting point. Measure camber, loosen the inboard nut approximately two turns, then slide the control arm inboard or outboard to change the reading. Recheck the alignment to verify the change and adjust rear toe if needed. The supplied procedure lists a torque of 76 lb.-ft. (103 Nm) for the upper control arm inboard nut.

Rear toe is adjusted at the toe link. With the steering wheel held straight ahead, measure toe on both sides. Before turning the toe-link bolt, clean the area around the joint using mild liquids. Ford notes that the cam nut and cam bolt area must be free of foreign material for proper clamping. Loosen the toe-link nut approximately one turn, rotate the toe-link bolt to obtain the specified reading, and tighten without disturbing the setting. The procedure lists 66 lb.-ft. (90 Nm) for the toe-link nut.

If the Mach-E is equipped with Lane Departure Warning, Ford requires an IPMA camera alignment after rear toe adjustment. Connect a scan tool and follow its directions for the camera alignment procedure. Road test after the adjustment and required camera service.

The supplied ride-height procedure uses a surface gauge to measure from a flat, level surface to suspension reference points. At the front, measure from the surface to the center of the lower arm forward bolt and to the center of the ball-joint pinch bolt. Subtract the lower-arm forward-bolt measurement from the ball-joint pinch-bolt measurement to calculate front ride height.

At the rear, measure from the surface to the center of the lower arm-to-subframe bolt and to the center of the lower arm-to-wheel-knuckle bolt. For the rear, subtract the wheel-knuckle-bolt measurement from the subframe-bolt measurement.

The service information provided describes how to take these measurements but does not give target ride-height values. Use the correct model-year service information for the vehicle to determine whether the recorded measurements are within specification. Avoid substituting a visual estimate or a generic ride-height value.

The vehicle’s service information shows a headlamp level sensor at both the front and rear suspension. The front sensor is mounted at the left front suspension, with its arm bracket attached to the lower arm. The rear sensor is also mounted at the left side, with its arm bracket attached to the lower arm. Each has an electrical connector.

During a suspension or alignment inspection, check that the sensors, brackets, arms and wiring are present and undamaged. The supplied procedure covers sensor removal and installation, but it does not specify an adjustment or calibration following a wheel alignment. If a sensor or its linkage has been disturbed or damaged, consult the correct service information for the required repair steps.

Last year, Chinese and Turkish brake drum manufacturers were hit with antidumping duties for selling some trailer brake drums in the United States at less than fair market value. The news gave me flashbacks to the light-vehicle rotor market 25 years ago, when I first started working on Brake & Front End magazine.
In the early 2000s, shops faced brake pedal pulsation comebacks for several reasons. Some people might call it a perfect storm.

Facing new fuel-efficiency standards, OEMs began removing mass from brake rotors. Vehicles such as the Jeep Cherokee and Chevrolet Malibu used “composite” rotor designs with stamped-steel hats cast into iron friction rings. These rotors would develop lateral runout if the lug nuts were tightened even slightly unevenly.

Some rotor manufacturers introduced one-piece replacements for these composite applications, but wheel-stud length was always a concern. Because the cast hats were thicker, the studs sometimes did not extend far enough beyond the rotor flange to properly secure the wheel. Some aftermarket brake companies even offered longer wheel-stud kits.

This period also marked the infancy of ceramic brake pad formulations. Most OE friction materials at the start of the transition process were semi-metallic or aggressive non-asbestos organic (NAO) compounds that could contribute to disc thickness variation when even a small amounts of runout were present. Ceramic formulations were being rolled out that on new OE platforms and as aftermarket alternatives. They can be credited, at least in part, with extending rotor life and reducing incidents of brake pedal pulsation.

What I remember most was the debate surrounding replacement brake rotors. In the late 1990s, “offshore manufacturers” were selling brake rotors at prices well below fair market value. By 2006, the federal government had begun investigating the situation and imposed antidumping duties on certain imports.

Within the aftermarket, some brake brands alleged that these inexpensive rotors were unsafe. Their main argument was that manufacturers were reducing rotor weight by making the friction plates thinner and failing to match the original fin design. I remember several press events that highlighted these design differences. I also remember phone calls from other rotor manufacturers arguing that the practice was acceptable because OE rotors were designed with an “eight-times” safety margin.

The lasting effect of these events were on technicians and repair shops. Replacement brake rotors became so inexpensive that installing new ones often cost less than the labor required to machine the originals. The economics allowed shops to recommend new rotors with increasing frequency, based on the rationale that replacement produced a more reliable, comeback-free brake job.

This replacement mindset even prompted California’s Bureau of Automotive Repair to conduct a sting investigation in 2010 targeting shops that recommended new rotors without first measuring the thickness of the existing ones.

Like it or not, we have been spoiled by inexpensive brake rotors over the past 20 years. Their availability permanently changed how some technicians and shops service brake systems. Today, it is not uncommon for technicians to recommend new rotors regardless of whether the existing rotors remain within specification, based on the economics.

The market, however, is always changing. Vehicle brake systems have improved, and modern friction formulations have extended rotor life through better ceramic transfer-layer developments. OEMs have also increased the size and mass of many brake rotors to improve braking performance, manage heat and control noise.

On the parts side, replacement rotor prices have increased because of higher transportation costs, inflation, tariffs and other market pressures. Rotors have also become more sophisticated, incorporating improved hat and heat-dam designs. Coatings and treatments such as ferritic nitrocarburizing have further increased the price of replacement rotors.

In my opinion, we are approaching another perfect storm. As replacement rotor prices rise and original brake rotors become more durable, the economics of replacement versus machining are beginning to converge on some brake jobs—especially when shops compare labor and parts costs while accounting for the rotor’s discard dimension.

As an industry veteran who survived the rotor wars, I see this as a win-win for repair shops. On the labor side, machining rotors can be a profitable again. On the parts side, selling a higher-value replacement rotor can generate more gross-profit dollars.
It may be time to dust off your micrometers and tune up your brake lathes.

The BMW N53 (naturally aspirated) and N54 (turbocharged) engines were among the first BMW engines to come with variable valve timing on the intake and exhaust camshafts. The N53 and N54 straight-six have unfairly earned a bad reputation for reliability with technicians due to timing chain and variable valve timing problems. The reputation comes from owners not keeping up with oil changes and it is difficult to check engine timing.

The latest versions continuously adjust the position of the intake and exhaust camshafts for better power, efficiency and idle performance. The keyword to remember for a late-model VANOS system is that it works “continuously,” and not just under specific RPM ranges.

To service them, you will need the appropriate toolset to lock the crank and camshaft. You will also need a scan tool and scope to observe the crankshaft and camshaft signals to accomplish more advanced diagnostics.

Some newer systems can change the camshaft timing by as much as ±72 degrees. Dual-VANOS systems operate at all engine speeds. At lower engine speeds, the VANOS system opens the valves later during the intake stroke, increasing the vacuum and scavenging effect generated by the piston traveling downward in the cylinder. This improves idle quality and smooth power tip-in from a stop. As the engine rpm increases, the valves are opened earlier, enhancing torque as rpm increases. At higher engine speeds, the valves open later for full power delivery so the scavenging effect of the exhaust leaving the cylinder can pull more air into the cylinder. Hot rodders call this “valve overlap.”
The system can augment and even eliminate the EGR valve by allowing some of the exhaust gas to remain in the combustion chamber to control combustion temperatures and NOX emissions.

Also, the camshaft position is changed to reduce engine warm-up times by allowing some unburned fuel to reach the catalytic converters. When the VANOS system on the N53 and N54 is not working, the most common symptoms are poor idle quality, reduced power and poor fuel economy. These symptoms are common to any other variable valve timing system, as well.
Like many variable valve timing systems, VANOS uses oil pressure-powered actuators to move the camshafts. The actuators need a consistent supply of oil for the correct viscosity, pressure and volume.
The N53 and N54 use a conventional cam phaser with internal chambers that hold pressurized oil that changes the position of the camshaft.
BMW N53 and N54 use an oil control valve like a lot of other variable valve timing engines. The solenoid is actuated by a pulse-width modulated signal.

If the oil is contaminated or is the wrong viscosity, the system can become sluggish. If the oil pressure can’t move the camshafts to the target positions in a specified time, the camshaft position sensors will sense it and set a code.

When oil pressure is not present, the camshafts go to a fully retarded position and are locked in place by a pin. A code will be set if the actuator and camshaft do not return to the correct position, because they are hydraulically jammed due to oil pressure leaking past a seal.

Disconnect the oil control valve if you are trying to scope a crankshaft and camshaft waveform. If this is not done, the waveform might look like the timing is out of sync because the engine will be adjusting the camshafts.
What Goes Wrong With N53 And N54 VANOS Systems?

The two most common failures for a VANOS system are related to the quality of the oil. The most common failure is when the O-ring seal on the piston wears out and allows oil pressure to move between the two chambers. This causes the actuator to be stuck or hydraulically jammed in either the full advance or retard positions.
When this happens, the actuator can’t fight the pressure exerted on the camshaft by the valve springs. This can cause a rattling noise at startup and idle.

If the oil is the wrong viscosity, it can cause the corrections to either retard or advance – in other words, to lag or happen too quickly. These changes take place in milliseconds. Depending on your scan tool and whether you can pull BMW DME or OBDII codes, the description may include the words jammed, stiff or lagging.

The engine will factor in the oil and coolant temperature into the time allowed for the actuation. If you have any codes related to these sensors, you might want to resolve these issues before troubleshooting the VANOS system.

Remind your customers that the quality of the oil in both engines matters to the life of their timing chains. BMW recommends a high-quality 5W-30 or 5W-40 that is fully synthetic and meets the BMW Longlife-01 FE specifications. These oils are formulated around the extended oil change interval. When a low-quality oil is used, it can break down before the oil change interval and accelerate wear on the links and pins of the timing chain.

LED headlights are changing the role of forward illumination. Before LEDs, forward lighting was just a bulb that cast its light in a pattern defined by the housing. Most of the innovation came with incandescent, halogen and Xenon bulbs. But light-emitting diodes (LEDs) are really a game changer for designers, engineers and technicians.

LED lights offer increased functionality by being able to control the brightness and pattern almost instantaneously. This is the case with Audi’s Matrix LED headlights found on the A8 and some E-Tron models. With these headlights, just the high-beam unit itself is made up of 25 individual segments. The small light-emitting diodes, which work in conjunction with lenses and reflectors connected in series, are activated and deactivated or dimmed individually according to the situation. This enables the system to react precisely to other cars, which it recognizes using a camera, and always illuminates the road brightly. Additional features of the new headlights are the intelligent cornering light, new-look daytime running lights and dynamic turn signals. The Audi Matrix LED headlights get the information they need from a camera, the navigation system and other sensors.

Composed of 1.3 million micromirrors per headlight, the units operate like movie projectors, emitting tiny unique particles or adaptable light. This is done with electrostatically controlled micromirrors that can adjust light beam pixels up to 5,000 times per second.

This lighting technology offers a selection of five different welcome/leaving animations when the vehicle is parked, each with unique motion graphics and text selected through the vehicle’s touchscreen display.

Audi’s lighting technology provides drivers with a 50-meter “light carpet” that is designed to keep light within the driver’s lane and extends the carpet left or right when changing lanes, and helps to avoid a “blinding” effect for oncoming traffic. Low-beam curved lighting bends below oncoming traffic, helping to illuminate people or objects on the side of the road that are otherwise difficult to detect. And on-ground light arrows help place the vehicle’s tires within its lane.

Early versions from 2020 in the U.S. lacked functions of the light carpet due to antiquated headlight laws that forbid adaptive lighting. Previously, the system could only show logos during startup and shutdown. On recent models, most of the European functionality has been enabled due to changes in headlight laws and adaptive lighting.

The good news is that the LED segments and lighting elements are expected to last the lifetime of the vehicle. But the units are sealed, and individual components inside can’t be serviced. The complete headlight assembly may cost in excess of $6,000 to replace.

The units are deeply integrated with the ADAS systems of the vehicle, including the Pre-Sense systems for automatic emergency braking. Having a scan tool that can talk to the ADAS system’s modules is critical. The ability to program replacement is also vital. Audi has issued several updates over the air and in new calibrations from the service information website.
The headlights are aimed and calibrated using a dynamic self-learning procedure that uses the forward-facing camera. If the camera is out of calibration, the headlights might not be aimed properly.

That approach also extends to data, an area where Magnaflow has made significant investments. By controlling more of the process and supply chain, Paolone said the company gains flexibility while supporting its long-term strategy. Looking ahead, Paolone sees significant growth opportunities across Magnaflow’s existing emissions and exhaust business, BRExhaust and its expanding OE business. The company models vehicle trends through 2040 and expects hybrids, which still require catalytic converters and exhaust systems, to create additional opportunities. BRExhaust is also expanding by offering complete installation kits for repair shops that eliminate the need for welding, cutting or pipe bending, helping technicians complete more repairs in-house. Walking into a major automotive trade show for the first time can feel overwhelming. Hundreds of companies are displaying tools, equipment, technology and vehicles. Industry professionals are everywhere, and there’s more to see than you can cover in a single day.

The automotive industry is changing quickly. Today’s technicians need to understand traditional mechanical systems along with advanced electronics, vehicle networks, driver-assistance systems and electrified powertrains.

But if you’re studying automotive technology, a trade show is more than a chance to check out cool cars and the latest tools. It’s an opportunity to learn how the industry works, discover career paths and connect with people who could help you land your first job.

Whether you’re attending a national event like the SEMA Show or AAPEX, or visiting a regional automotive training expo, a little preparation can turn your experience into something valuable for your future.
Trade shows give you a closer look at how manufacturers, equipment suppliers and experienced technicians are responding to those changes.
You may get to see diagnostic tools in action, learn about new repair procedures or speak directly with the people who design the equipment used in professional shops.

Trade shows can also introduce you to career opportunities you might not have considered. Beyond working as a technician, the automotive industry offers roles in technical training, engineering, equipment development, service management and technical support.
Your goal shouldn’t be to see everything. It should be to leave knowing more than you did when you arrived.
Trade shows can cover enormous exhibition spaces. Without a plan, you could spend most of your time walking around instead of learning.
Start by reviewing the event’s website, exhibitor list and educational schedule. Identify the companies and training sessions that match your interests.

If you’re interested in diagnostics, look for scan tool manufacturers, testing equipment suppliers and demonstrations involving electrical systems. If you enjoy performance work, explore engine technology, drivetrain components and vehicle modification equipment.
Choose five companies or exhibits you want to visit, three questions you’d like answered and at least one educational session that could strengthen your technical knowledge.

Download the event app or save the floor map to your phone, if available. You should also check registration requirements, age restrictions, student opportunities and any required safety equipment for demonstrations.
If you’re attending with your automotive class, ask your instructor whether there’s a specific assignment or learning objective for the trip.
2. Focus on Technology You’ll See in the Shop
One of the biggest benefits of attending an automotive trade show is seeing how classroom concepts connect to real repair work.
Many events feature demonstrations that help explain the tools and procedures technicians use to solve problems.
- Advanced diagnostics: Watch how technicians use scan tools, oscilloscopes and electrical testing equipment to identify faults rather than simply replace parts.
- Electric and hybrid vehicles: Learn about high-voltage safety, battery systems, insulated tools and the training required before servicing electrified vehicles.
- ADAS technology: Explore the equipment used to calibrate cameras, radar sensors and other advanced driver-assistance systems.
- Tire and wheel service: Look for tire pressure monitoring system (TPMS) tools, tire inspection equipment and wheel alignment technology.
- Air conditioning systems: Learn about refrigerant identification, leak detection and service equipment designed for modern vehicles.
- Connected vehicles and software: Ask how digital service information, vehicle networks and software updates affect repair procedures.

For example, if your class recently covered electrical circuit testing, find a demonstration involving voltage drop testing or oscilloscope waveforms. Compare what you’re seeing with the diagnostic process your instructor taught you.
Don’t just watch the demonstration. Try to understand why the technician performs each step.
Ask questions such as, “How would you verify this failure in a real shop?” or “What mistakes do new technicians commonly make with this procedure?”
These conversations can help turn a product demonstration into a practical learning experience.
3. Don’t Be Afraid to Talk to Industry Professionals
You don’t need years of shop experience to start a conversation at a trade show. In fact, many exhibitors welcome the opportunity to talk with students entering the industry.
Introduce yourself, explain what you’re studying and ask a thoughtful question.
“Hi, I’m an automotive technology student, and we’re currently learning about electrical diagnostics. Can you explain how this tool would help identify an intermittent problem?”
This tells the exhibitor that you’re genuinely interested in learning, not just collecting free merchandise.
- What skills should entry-level technicians develop first?
- What types of diagnostic problems does your equipment help solve?
- What training resources are available for students?
- How is this technology changing what technicians do?
- What would you recommend to someone preparing for their first automotive job?
Listen carefully and don’t worry if you don’t understand every technical term. Asking for clarification is part of learning.
Remember, the person you’re speaking with might be a technician, engineer, trainer, recruiter or business owner. Each can offer a different perspective on the industry.
4. Use the Show to Explore Your Career Options
A trade show can also serve as an introduction to the professional side of the automotive industry.
Many students think their career options begin and end with working in a dealership or independent repair shop. Those are important paths, but they’re not the only ones.
Automotive professionals also work for tool manufacturers, parts suppliers, vehicle manufacturers, training organizations and equipment companies.
Some began their careers turning wrenches before moving into technical support, product testing, training or management.
If a particular company interests you, ask what its entry-level career paths look like.
You can also ask whether the company offers internships, apprenticeships, scholarships or technical training opportunities.
Prepare a short introduction about yourself.
You don’t need a formal speech. Be ready to explain what you’re studying, which automotive systems interest you and what kind of experience you’re hoping to gain.

If you’re actively looking for work, bring a simple resume or have a digital copy available on your phone. Include your automotive coursework, relevant certifications, shop experience and technical skills.
A professional LinkedIn profile can also help you stay connected with people you meet.
5. Take Advantage of Student Programs and Training
Some major automotive trade shows provide opportunities specifically for students and instructors.

The SEMA Show Student Program introduces students to automotive aftermarket careers and includes opportunities to connect with industry professionals. AAPEX also offers student programming focused on industry exposure, education and networking.
These programs can make large trade shows easier to navigate, especially if you’re attending for the first time.
Look for educational seminars, skills competitions, student networking events and demonstrations aimed at beginning technicians.
Training sessions can be especially valuable when they reinforce topics you’re already studying, such as electrical diagnosis, braking systems or engine performance.
Before registering, verify eligibility requirements, deadlines and whether your school needs to coordinate attendance.
If you’re unable to travel to a major national event, check for regional training expos, career fairs, technical competitions and distributor-sponsored training events closer to home.
The same skills—asking questions, observing demonstrations and meeting professionals—apply at smaller events.
6. Be Professional, Even If You’re Just There to Learn
You don’t need to wear a suit to a trade show, but your appearance and behavior should reflect someone preparing to enter a professional industry.

Wear clean, comfortable clothes and shoes suitable for spending several hours on your feet. Some events may recommend business-casual attire, while specific demonstrations may have additional safety requirements.
Keep your student badge visible and respect exhibitor displays. Ask permission before handling tools, entering vehicles or recording demonstrations.
Pay attention when someone is explaining a product. If an exhibitor is speaking with a customer, wait for an appropriate time to ask your question.
And while there’s nothing wrong with picking up a few giveaways, don’t make free merchandise the focus of your visit.
A professional attitude can leave an impression long after the event is over.
Your smartphone can be one of your most useful tools at a trade show.
Use it to save session schedules, record notes, scan QR codes and organize information about products or companies you want to research later.
If recording is permitted, take short videos of demonstrations that relate to your coursework. Capture the important steps rather than trying to film everything.
For example, after watching a diagnostic demonstration, write down:
- What vehicle problem was being diagnosed?
- Which tool or testing method was used?
- What measurements helped identify the problem?
- How did the technician verify the repair or diagnosis?
- What would you like to learn more about?
These notes can help you review the information with your instructor or classmates.
You can also use digital tools to organize what you’ve learned, but remember to verify technical information against trusted service procedures and training materials.
A quick online summary is no substitute for understanding how a system actually works.
Your trade-show experience shouldn’t end when you leave the convention center.
Within a few days, review your notes and identify the most useful things you learned.
If someone shared helpful career advice or explained a technical concept, send a brief thank-you message through email or LinkedIn.
Mention where you met and what you discussed. A personal message is more meaningful than a generic connection request.
Then take what you’ve learned back to the classroom or shop.
For example, if you watched a demonstration of an oscilloscope being used to diagnose a sensor problem, ask your instructor whether you can practice a similar testing procedure in the lab.
If you learned about a new career path, research the skills and certifications commonly associated with that role.
Turn what you saw at the show into something you can practice, research or apply.
9. Challenge Yourself to Leave With Three Things
Before you attend your next trade show, set three simple goals:
One new technical skill or concept. Learn something you can explain to your instructor or demonstrate in the shop.
One professional connection. Meet someone who can help you better understand the industry or a possible career path.
One next step. Identify a training course, certification goal, internship opportunity or technical skill you want to pursue.
You don’t need to return home knowing everything about the automotive industry. You just need to make progress toward becoming a better technician.
Your Career Starts Before Your First Full-Time Job
Automotive trade shows give students an opportunity to see where the industry is headed and what skills they’ll need to succeed.

The technology on display might eventually become equipment you use every day. The diagnostic procedures you observe could help you solve a difficult problem in the shop. And the professional you meet might help point you toward your first job.
Go prepared, stay curious and ask questions. Make connections, take notes and put what you’ve learned into practice.

Repair planning tips, how to document OEM repair procedures and get paid for following them, and in-house mechanical work — those are just three of several topics covered during the Society of Collision Repair Specialists (SCRS) Repairer Driven Education (RDE) sessions at this year’s SEMA Show.

Justin Lewis, president of Accurate Auto Body in Washington, will lead “Reclaiming Technical Authority: Earning Consumer Authorization,” focused on the collision repair shop’s role in repair planning.

“The whole point of the presentation is essentially to establish the shop is building a repair plan that the customer is the person authorizing that, and the insurer’s role is indemnification,” Lewis said. “And too many times shops are relying on the insurer’s cost estimate to dictate repairs and giving up their technical authority. In turn, it’s causing them liability issues.”
He added that the session will explain how shops can:
- Gain customer authorization to make repair decisions in their best interest;
- Support documentation with OEM repair procedures; and
- Separate those three items so that one doesn’t control the other.
Lewis said he’ll cover what proper documentation looks like, when and how thoroughly to complete it, and how to get the customer’s buy-in.
Backing up repair plans with documented OEM repair procedures and explaining that process builds a foundation of trust with customers, Lewis said.

“Just because an insurer disagrees doesn’t necessarily mean that it’s not something that’s required or necessary to fix the car right, and then how to support your customer in that situation,” he said.

Lewis also plans to touch on the right to appraisal and minimum standards for insurer claims handling that took effect earlier this week in Washington. After six years of advocating by the Washington Independent Collision Repair Association (WICRA) for mandatory right to appraisal, Gov. Bob Ferguson signed it into law last year.
While Lewis’s session name mentions the technical side of customer authorization, he said he plans to keep it simple.

“My intention is to make people think, ‘Oh, I’m matching insurance sheets. I shouldn’t be doing that,'” he said. “One of my big things in there is this industry made a change. It went from what’s required to fix the car to what the insurance is willing to pay, and that’s not the right way to address repair requirements. That’s going to be the whole premise: getting the mindset changed from will they pay for it to what’s required and what’s my liability if I don’t do it. What does the OEM say I have to do versus what does the insurance want to indemnify? And then how do I get my customer to authorize what needs to be done, and how do I support that?”

Isaac Aronson’s “Repair Planning That Pays: Protecting Revenue Through Research” session will cover the inconsistencies of collision repair planning from the perspective of front-end research behaviors. Aronson, OEConnection’s product manager, will discuss how those behaviors translate into measurable financial outcomes.

“Modern vehicles require extensive OEM research, conditional procedure evaluation, and calibration consideration before repairs even begin,” the session description states. “Yet inconsistent workflows create supplements, delays, and lost revenue opportunities for performed work.”

Based on patterns across thousands of repair plans, Aronson will identify where breakdowns most commonly occur and how early research decisions influence final profitability, such as including calibration evaluation into a structured workflow.

A panel discussion centered on mechanical repairs will include Steve Dawson, Hunter Engineering regional manager; Todd Hesford, owner of Mission Viejo Auto Collision; Dan Stander, president of Fix Auto Highlands Ranch; Chris Dacus, owner of Dacus Auto Body and Collision Repair; and Gerry McNee, owner of Ultimate Collision Repair.
Titled “Bringing Mechanical Repairs In-house,” the session will candidly cover what transitioning to in-house availability entails, according to the session description.

“More collision repair businesses are evaluating whether bringing mechanical work in-house can create new revenue opportunities, improve cycle time, and strengthen control over the repair process,” the description states. “But what does that transition really look like in practice?”

SCRS notes that the panelists are from high-performing shops, and they’ll share why they decided to expand into mechanical repairs, how they implemented the change, and what impact it has had on their operations and profitability.
